title: Penn State’s defense had to ‘change everything’ about practice, emphasizing tackling
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Safety Jeremiah Cooper said the defense was “disgusted” and “sick” after watching the game film from Penn State’s loss to Northwestern, calling the performance “embarrassing."

There were a lot of missed tackles in the 413-yard showing on the ground by the Wildcats, and part of that was due to practice not being physical enough, something wide receiver Chase Sowell and tight end Benjamin Brahmer discussed postgame.

So in an effort to get things back on track ahead of the White Out against USC, D’Anton Lynn installed more tackling drills into practice.

“Everything is just ramped up right now,” Cooper said Wednesday. “We had to change everything. The intensity stepped up this week in practice, and we all felt it.”

While the players admitted their mistakes on the field, Lynn said he and the coaching staff didn’t include as many tackling drills as he wanted to because of the shortened week.

“We have to figure out different drills to put these guys in better positions,” Lynn said Tuesday. “However it gets done, it's our job to make sure it gets done.”

Lynn identified specific aspects of tackling Penn State struggled with against Northwestern, including tackling in space, in the hole and when the ball gets outside of the cornerbacks. He said those areas have and will continue to be accounted for in practice.

He also shared how tackling isn’t a static skill a defense can possess. Instead, it’s based on the effectiveness of each week’s practice regimen and how the defense prepares for the specific opponent.

“I always say just because you tackle good in games doesn't mean you're a good tackling team,” Lynn said. “Because you have a game like this, all of a sudden you're a bad tackling team. Then we could tackle good next week, and we're a good tackling team again.”

Lynn said he’s emphasized tackling on both defense and special teams this week, using different drills to better suit the individual players. Due to this focus, linebacker Cael Brezina said Tuesday’s session was “the most physical practice we’ve had in a long time.”

Most of the team’s practice periods are “thud,” meaning the defenders engage in contact but don’t fall to the ground. Cooper said practice isn’t about throwing the opponent to the turf, but ensuring the team’s tackling mechanics are up to standard.

“It’s one-on-one drills, open field tackling,” Cooper said. “When we get in the team setting, instead of just tagging off the scout team, running backs, or whoever we're going against, we're hitting them, wrapping them up, driving our feet, emphasizing the little things.”

Brezina said executing those mechanics isn’t solely related to the point of contact, as the Nittany Lions have been working on the entire tackling process from start to finish after a two-game skid.

“Tackling is as much on the point of attack as it is everything leading up to a tackle,” Brezina said. “Getting better reps throughout the whole process of tackling is something that was really emphasized (Tuesday) and has to be emphasized going forward.”

One of the biggest questions heading into the White Out is whether Penn State has truly fixed its tackling issues, and only time will tell as running backs King Miller and Waymond Jordan look to establish a solid ground game for the Trojans.

However, Cooper was clear on how the defense needs to move forward amidst turmoil.

“We’ve got to keep working, ignore the outside noise,” Cooper said. “We all know what we messed up on and what we gotta work on. That just started at practice.”

title: Rocco Becht named to Johnny Unitas Golden Arm Award Top 15
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Rocco Becht's redshirt senior season is continuing to take shape.

Becht was named to the Johnny Unitas Golden Arm Award Top 15 list on Thursday, given annually to the best upperclassman quarterback in college football.

The former Iowa State quarterback was named to the watch list in August for the second straight year.

Through five games, Becht has thrown for 1,108 yards and 10 touchdowns with just three interceptions.

title: Former Penn State RB Kaytron Allen waived by Washington Commanders
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
One of Penn State's top all-time running backs has been let go from their NFL team midway through their rookie season.

Running back Kaytron Allen was waived by the Washington Commanders, the team announced Thursday.

He saw minimal action in three games so far this season in Washington, with 12 carries for 41 yards and a long of nine. His best performance came in Week 2 against the Dallas Cowboys when he had five rushes for 24 yards.

title: D’Anton Lynn’s return to Penn State as defensive coordinator ‘almost like a fairy tale’
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
When former Penn State defensive back Mike Wallace took his official visit to Happy Valley, then-cornerback D’Anton Lynn was the player who showed him what it meant to be a Nittany Lion.

Lynn made Wallace feel at home as he introduced him to the campus and team. The experience became a big reason Wallace chose Penn State and began a friendship that lasted well beyond their playing careers.

Nearly two decades later, Lynn is Penn State’s defensive coordinator, embodying many of the same characteristics that drew Wallace to the program in the first place.

“He’s the best fit because he’s best in class,” Wallace told The Daily Collegian. “He’s the perfect example for what his players and what the organization can model to continue pushing the Penn State football legacy. He's the paradigm of what Penn State football culture is.”

Lynn joined the Nittany Lions in 2008 and immediately saw the field, playing in nine games as a freshman. While he didn’t contribute much statistically, he used the opportunity to grow and earned more playing time the following year.

“He was really a genius in the film room,” Wallace said. “That rubbed off on everybody. He had a very studious nature about him from the very beginning.”

As Lynn began to see the field more regularly and become even more of an asset to Penn State’s defense, the contrast between him as a person and player became clear.

Wallace said Lynn was “like Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde” on and off the field. Lynn was a friendly face across the entire roster and connected with every player no matter their role.

“If you get to know him, there's so much joy in his heart,” Wallace said. “He has a big, infectious smile and when he sees you, he lights up. He has a lot of joy and a lot of love for the people that he loves.”

But when Lynn took the field, a switch flipped, and his friendly persona disappeared.

Lynn was aggressive, and that translated into success throughout Lynn’s four years in Happy Valley, as he was a three-time All-Big Ten honorable mention and finished second in tackles among the team and tied for first in interceptions his junior year.

“On the field, he was a nut,” Wallace said. “Just an absolute crazy man. You wouldn’t expect that out of him if you just knew him in the classroom, but the reason why he was so good was because he was a very aggressive player.”

After four years at Penn State, Lynn had a brief professional career, spending a year with the New York Jets and a year in the Canadian Football League. From there, he transitioned into coaching, something Wallace knew he’d excel at.

“It didn’t surprise me, because he was always super intelligent,” Wallace said. “He almost looked like a player coach the same way LeBron (James) is now. He was always a leader on the field, but also somebody who was constantly teaching.”

Lynn eventually held position coaching roles with the Jets, Buffalo Bills, Los Angeles Chargers, Houston Texans and Baltimore Ravens.

He didn’t know where coaching would ultimately take him, but each stop offered another opportunity for Lynn to learn from different coaches and coordinators, eventually developing a style of his own.

“Each team that you coach with, you take bits and pieces,” Lynn said Aug. 7. “I started off with Rex Ryan and kind of got exposed to everything, but it’s a collection of all those. Each coordinator I’ve been with has been different in their own way.”

In 2023, Lynn made the move to college, becoming the defensive coordinator at UCLA before taking over USC’s defense a year later. He spent two seasons with the Trojans before Matt Campbell reached out about the open defensive coordinator spot he had after he was hired at Penn State. They had a nearly two-hour phone call where Lynn said Campbell “reminded me of why I came to Penn State as a player out of high school” and offered him the job, which Lynn accepted quickly after.

“When I got off the phone with him, there was just something in my gut that told me that this just felt right,” Lynn said. “I told my wife, ‘I don’t know how it’s going to work, but somehow, some way, I just feel like we need to make this work.’”

Lynn’s choice to return to his alma mater provided him an opportunity to give back to the program that shaped him.

“This place obviously had a lot to do with my development and who I am today,” Lynn said. “I didn’t think I’d get a chance to come back here and be able to give back. So to be able to be here and see things from a different perspective and be able to coach now and give back to the players has been awesome.”

Through his first few months with the program, Lynn has established a simple defense he’s said will grow in complexity as the season progresses. But even though he has nearly 10 years of NFL coaching experience and three seasons as a defensive coordinator, Lynn has remained receptive to his players’ input.

Tony Rojas, who has had four different defensive coordinators in four years at Penn State, even went as far to say Lynn has been the first of the four he’s had a personal connection with.

“What makes him a great teacher is his understanding of how the student thinks and processes information,” defensive tackle Siale Taupaki said Aug. 25. “There’s certain things that he wants done, but then his doors are always open for us to come up and be like ‘Coach, I think this, I think that.’”

As Penn State’s season has progressed, its defense has experienced its share of highs and lows. Lynn has remained the same steady presence through it all, showcasing the qualities Wallace saw in him as a teammate.

With the Trojans coming to town on Saturday, Lynn will face his former program in his first White Out as a coach. He said Tuesday that he still loves “all the people” at USC, but is happy where he is now.

And he’s not the only one thrilled, as Lynn’s reunion with Penn State is a celebration for those who’ve been with him throughout his career.

“It was a full circle moment for him to get the job back at Penn State,” Wallace said. “It was such a catalyst for all of us to rally behind the team because our teammate came back to the place where it all started. It’s beautiful, almost like a fairy tale. It means the world.”

title: Staff predictions | Can Penn State use the White Out against USC to get back in the win column?
author: The Daily Collegian football staff
description:
The most-anticipated game of Penn State’s season is almost here, although it’s not the matchup many thought it would be.

No. 19 USC is headed to Happy Valley for the annual White Out, marking the Nittany Lions first ranked opponent this year. The Trojans will be a tough task for Penn State’s defense with one of the better quarterbacks in the Big Ten and a high-scoring offense, although they’ve had their fair share of struggles defensively.

Can Penn State upset USC and win its first conference game of 2026?

Andrew Deal: Penn State 27, USC 21

USC has struggled in cross-country games, and even with the game beginning at night, I still think the Trojans start out slow.

The battle when Penn State’s defense is on the field will be interesting to watch throughout the game, as D’Anton Lynn has faced USC quarterback Jayden Maiava in practice all of last year. On the flip side, USC’s offense faced Lynn’s defense, so the potential chess match could decide the game.

The main battle will be the Trojan’s passing attack against Penn State’s pass defense, with both ranked among the best in the country in terms of yards per game. With the cornerback strength, the Nittany Lions hold the advantage despite not facing receivers at the caliber of USC’s.

Penn State’s offense will find enough success for it to hold a lead in the fourth quarter, featuring the tight ends early and often as it finds a rhythm for the first time in two games.

The defense will hold up enough against USC’s dynamic offense, and I think the Nittany Lions will come out on top to earn their first Big Ten win of the season.

Andrew Mercer: USC 35, Penn State 31

Penn State learned a lot in the loss to Northwestern last week, and although I believe the Nittany Lions will put in a stronger performance, I don’t believe they’ll get over the hump.

A good chunk of Matt Campbell’s guys will be experiencing their first White Out game. Linebacker Kooper Ebel and defensive tackle Keanu Williams mentioned difficulties dealing with crowd noise against Wisconsin, and Penn State’s signature game is exponentially louder than that.

Lynn’s “obnoxious communication” has been a point of emphasis throughout the season, so if the team couldn’t figure it out against the Badgers, I doubt it’ll be any better against the Trojans. Therefore, I believe running backs King Miller and Waymond Jordan are going to exploit the Nittany Lions’ failing run defense.

I have Rocco Becht returning to form in the White Out. While he was inconsistent in both losses, he showed flashes of connection with wide receiver Chase Sowell, and if he can spin the ball to tight end Benjamin Brahmer more often, the offense will find more success.

Besides, USC gave up 21 points to Washington last week, which has a struggling offense, so I think Penn State can surpass that mark. However, a semi-successful offense is nothing without a top-tier defense, so quarterback Jayden Maiava will likely avoid Penn State’s cornerbacks en route to a tight victory.

Lexie Linderman: USC 31, Penn State 27

The biggest question heading into this game is whether Lynn’s defense can hold up against his former team.

USC’s offense is one of the best in the Big Ten, averaging 467.8 yards per game. Penn State’s defense is coming off its worst performance of the year, allowing 31 points and 413 rushing yards to Northwestern.

Luckily for the Nittany Lions, the Trojans are averaging 156.2 rushing yards per game, which is just barely behind Penn State’s rushing attack, meaning USC relies heavily on its quarterback Jayden Maiava.

The Nittany Lions’ secondary is elite, only allowing two total passing touchdowns this year, both of which came from Wisconsin’s Colton Joseph. So, that could make things difficult for Maiava and Lincoln Riley’s offense.

But I still think USC’s firepower is too much for Penn State, which has really struggled on offense during Big Ten play. That will ultimately be the deciding factor, as the Nittany Lions will come up just short against their first top-25 opponent of the year.

Noah Aberegg: USC 34, Penn State 24

Penn State’s struggles have been apparent over the last two weeks. After recognizing those issues following the loss to Wisconsin, things only seemed to get worse against Northwestern.

While talks in the Lasch Building make it sound like the Nittany Lions are ready to flip the switch, I don’t think that will necessarily translate to Campbell’s first Big Ten win against one of the better offenses in the conference.

The Nittany Lions’ secondary is also among the best in the Big Ten, but Maiava is too good of a quarterback and Riley is too good of a coach to let that stop them. He’ll throw for multiple touchdowns as the running backs will also find success against Penn State’s struggling run defense.

I think Becht will have his best game since conference play began and will also throw for multiple touchdowns — the first time since Sept. 19 against Buffalo.

While the offense will see improvement, Koby Howard’s continued absence will be an issue yet again as explosive plays will be slow to develop. However, USC has allowed the fourth-most passing yards per game in the Big Ten, and Sowell, Brahmer and wide receiver Brett Eskildsen.

The run game won’t find the success it did against Buffalo, but I think it has the potential to have a much better performance than the last two weeks. Running back James Peoples will be announced as a starter for the first time in Beaver Stadium, and he’ll find the end zone for the third time this year.

title: Bonfatto’s Italian Market and Corner Cafe changes lives in one sip and one bite
author: Talia Rittenhouse | The Daily Collegian
description:
Bonfatto’s Italian Market and Corner Cafe offers delicious meals, pastries, lattes and products for purchase.

This Italian cafe, located at 401 W. High St, Bellefonte, Pennsylvania, just a short 15-minute drive from downtown State College, is by far worth the drive.

From breakfast to lunch, snacks and caffeinated drinks, Bonfatto's is a great place for beginning your day, a date with a friend or a study session.

Inside the cafe, there are tables for you to sit and an amazing atmosphere built with natural lighting and inviting decor. You can also purchase Italian foods at the market part of this storefront, such as pasta, sauces, mozzarella, stuffed shells, charcuterie and more.

Toasted Marshmallow Latte

Taking even just one sip will change your life. The light flavor of marshmallow consumes the drink, reminding you of s’mores at a campfire.

The toasted marshmallow latte is so creamy from the milk and fits perfectly with the tone of the flavoring. I can’t say enough about how perfect this latte is.

It genuinely brought a smile to my face and brightened my mood with each sip of its sweet, light flavor.

Now, if you like to chug coffee, this is the one — the flavor isn’t too sweet, and with the creamy, smooth texture, it might be gone in a matter of minutes.

Rating: 10/10

Apple Crisp Latte

The apple crisp latte at Bonfatto’s matches its name perfectly. Through the authentic, clear apple, cinnamon and toasted flavor, it tastes like you're truly drinking a slice of apple crisp.

What I love about the lattes here is that Bonfatto’s espresso is not too bitter — it's smooth and does not overpower a drink, matches well with the latte flavors and is completed with creamy milk.

I got this latte with oat milk, but I think I would’ve enjoyed it more with whole milk or another variety, since the oat milk didn’t provide the same creaminess as the toasted marshmallow latte. Next time, I would make this change, and it would be even closer to perfect.

Rating 9/10

Bomboloni

Wow — I have never had a better donut than this bomboloni.

It’s round and normally filled with a flavored pastry cream inside, but I ordered one without.

I have never tasted a dough so soft. It was chewy, but yet so fluffy and airy — I couldn’t get enough of it. It was not too sweet at all. The dough had a light sweetness on its own, and the sugar on top was a perfect addition.

And might I add, I’m not much of a donut person, and this one truly changed my perspective. This soft donut, with its light sugar coating, was spectacular — I could go on and on.

Rating 11/10

Smoked Pancetta, Egg and Cheese

At Bonfatto’s, customers can custom-make their own egg and cheese sandwich.

With provolone cheese, you can choose to add either smoked pancetta, sweet Italian sausage or rosemary ham on a variety of different breads such as bagels, English muffins, croissants, focaccia, sourdough and more.

I got a smoked pancetta, egg and cheese on sourdough. The sourdough is soft on the inside but has a crispy exterior with a brushing of oil on top.

However, I think it might have been a bit better on another bread, like a croissant or a bagel, but that was just my personal preference for the textures of an egg sandwich.

Another perk of this dish was its size. At least for me, this was big enough that I was able to turn it into two meals. Each sourdough slice was about half a foot long, and, with the egg, cheese and pancetta inside, it was very filling.

Rating 8/10

Vodka Chicken Parm Panini

You know the cheese pull that everyone looks for in mozzarella sticks?

Well, Bonfatto’s chicken parm panini outdoes the cheese pull of any mozzarella stick I’ve ever had, as it's so stringy, gooey and flavorful.

This panini is again on the same sourdough as the egg and cheese sandwich, and is even more perfect in this meal. The oil on top combines with the Italian seasonings of the sauce, creating such great flavors in each bite, all with a crunch.

The vodka sauce is smooth, not so creamy that it would make your stomach ache, as a cheesy pasta might do, but just enough to perfect the classic vodka sauce flavor and texture.

The chicken cutlets are pounded thin and breaded, fulfilling the prophecy of the vodka chicken parm.

I would eat this meal every day if I could. Bonfatto’s perfected the flavors and textures so well I’d now prefer to have this dish in panini form forever.

Rating 10/10

title: Players to watch as No. 17 Penn State men’s hockey opens its season
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State lost numerous key pieces from its 2025-26 squad, including top NHL draft pick Gavin McKenna and Nashville Predators’ forward Aiden Fink. However, a strong group of returners sprinkled with transfer additions provides a strong core for the upcoming campaign.

Jackson Smith

The defenseman returns for a second season in Happy Valley after he set the Penn State record for goals by a blueliner with 11 last year. Smith, a Calgary, Alberta, native, earned second-team All-Big Ten honors and was named to the Big Ten All-Freshman Team.

This year, the first-round pick is expected to step into a new leadership role.

“He's Penn State through and through, which is fantastic,” Guy Gadowsky said at media day. “He's a guy that knows what it was like coming in the first time. He loves Penn State, and I think he knew the differences and how difficult the hard parts of transition were, what was easy and how it works, and he said, ‘I really want to help all the other guys that come from the CHL to quickly translate.’”

Justin Poirier

A new face in the forward room, Poirier transferred in from Maine this offseason. While in the Pine Tree State, Poirier tallied 29 points on 18 goals and 11 assists as a freshman.

The Salaberry-de-Valleyfield, Quebec, native said at local media day that while he enjoyed his year with the Black Bears, Big Ten hockey is closer to the professional level. Poirier also detailed his immediate love for Penn State that pulled him to University Park.

“I think Penn State is a great fit for me offensively,” Poirier said. “I came in for a visit and met the coaching staff, and I think it was the perfect fit for me to join Penn State.”

It’s been more of the same ever since he stepped on campus.

“We have a great leadership group,” Poirier said. “As soon as I transferred, again on my visit, I had two guys on the team that was here to just say hi to me and everything, to show me around, and I feel like that group is special so far.”

Gadowsky and Co. expect the 2024 fifth-round NHL Draft pick to continue acclimating quickly and contribute immediate offensive production, as he has at every previous level.

Dane Dowiak

Dowiak is set to become just the third Nittany Lion to rock the captain’s patch for multiple seasons. The Pittsburgh native finished his injury-shortened 2025-26 with a 54 percent faceoff win rate.

He suffered an upper body injury in February that required surgery, but said at media day that he returned to 100 percent in “early August.” Dowiak spent all offseason in State College rehabbing and preparing for his second year carrying the C.

“It hurt a lot to miss playoffs with the team and it being such a special group last year,” Dowiak said. “But I’m blessed to have another opportunity this year as a senior, and I’m grateful for the guys the coaches have brought in. I think it’s going to be a really good year.”

Mac Gadowsky

Gadowsky is one of the most decorated players on Penn State’s roster. The senior defenseman was an All-American and top-10 finalist for the Hobey Baker Award in his sophomore year at Army. He also led all defensemen in points and goals with 42 and 16, respectively.

In his first year at Penn State, Gadowsky took a significant step backward as a goal scorer, but held down the back line and starred in other phases of the game. The State College, Pennsylvania, native racked up 17 assists to just one goal and finished second on the team in blocked shots.

In addition to making the jump from Atlantic Hockey America to the Big Ten, Mac also had to adjust to playing for his father, Guy.

“It's been good getting to play for him, and being back home,” Mac Gadowsky said. “I definitely think that first year took a little bit. There was a little bit of awkwardness, I think, on my end. Just kind of looking up and being like, ‘Oh, there’s my dad, or he's my coach.’ So I think that I've kind of settled in, and the boys have all been great with that aspect as well.”

As a coach, Guy Gadowsky said they “expect him to be a leader at both ends of the ice.” As a father, Gadowsky just wants his son to start coming home for more Sunday dinners.

The Nittany Lions open their regular season on Friday night when they travel to take on No. 16 UConn at 7 p.m.

title: No. 17 Penn State men’s hockey opens 2026-27 season in Ice Breaker Tournament
author: Maggie Hardy | The Daily Collegian
description:
It’s been almost 200 days since Penn State’s season that was once filled with the hope of a national title ended with the final buzzer at the Albany Regional Semifinals at MVP Arena. Now, No. 17 Penn State is back for its 2026-27 campaign.

“When it’s game week, then everything just sort of feels good… I enjoy the adrenaline part of it,” head coach Guy Gadowsky said. “You know Thursday’s coming, and that’s when you've got to get ready to go, and everything’s just back on. It feels good.”

The Nittany Lions start their season on the road in the 30th annual Ice Breaker Tournament, which brings together four teams from across different conferences to open the college hockey season. No. 16 UConn and Sacred Heart will co-host, with Penn State and Bowling Green rounding out the field.

The blue and white begin Friday, with a 7 p.m. match against UConn at Toscano Family Ice Forum in Storrs, Connecticut, and finish Saturday at 7 p.m. against Sacred Heart at Martire Family Arena in Fairfield, Connecticut.

The new Nittany Lions

Penn State’s roster looks much different from the last time the team hit the ice back in March, after losing five of its top six scorers and a few key blueliners.

The Nittany Lions welcome 11 new faces to the squad this year, and with Gadowsky’s emphasis on “scoring by committee” this season as opposed to top-6 heavy production, the group has a chance to make an immediate impact up and down the lineup.

“The younger guys have been great. They fit in well, all the transfers as well,” captain Reese Laubach said. “Great for the culture. Great group of guys.”

Transfer forward Justin Poirier is expected to have a big season for the blue and white, after registering 29 points in 27 games during his freshman year at Maine.

In for returners, captain Dane Dowiak is back after suffering a season-ending upper-body injury in February and will most likely play an instrumental role on the team’s top line. Notable forwards Shea Van Olm and Luke Misa are also expected to take big developmental jumps as they enter their sophomore years.

On the back end, blueliner Jackson Smith proved himself as one of the best defensemen in the conference last season, and after being named to the Preseason All-Big Ten second team, he looks poised for another big year.

The Nittany Lions have also put together another strong goaltending tandem this season.

Sophomore Josh Fleming returns as the likely starter after posting an impressive .924 save percentage in his first season. Freshman Ryder Fetterolf is coming in as the clear backup after being named both the OHL and CHL Goaltender of the Year last season.

Scouting UConn

The last time these two teams met, it was etched in the history books as Penn State defeated UConn in overtime of the 2025 Allentown Regional Final, sending the program to its first-ever Frozen Four.

“They’re extremely structured and play really hard,” Gadowsky said. “That’s what we saw in Allentown, and that’s what I’m sure we’re going to see at UConn.”

The Huskies have had a lot of success in recent years, making it to both the Hockey East Championship and the NCAA Tournament in each of the last two seasons.

UConn, like the Nittany Lions, also saw significant roster turnover in the offseason.

The Huskies lost their leading goal scorer Ryan Tattle, captain Tabor Heaslip and starting goaltender Tyler Muszelik.

Ten newcomers — nine freshmen and one transfer student — joined UConn’s squad and will get a chance to debut against the Nittany Lions on Friday.

One of UConn’s biggest strengths is the return of forward Joey Muldowney for his senior season. Muldowney is a key part of the Huskies' offense, scoring 29 points in 34 games last season and earning second-team Hockey East All-Star honors.

Scouting Sacred Heart

Penn State has won all six previous contests against Sacred Heart, with the last meeting during the 2019-20 season.

The Pioneers are members of the Atlantic Hockey America conference and finished second last year behind Bentley with a 23-14-3 overall record.

Sacred Heart has a massive class of 17 newcomers this season, including 11 freshmen and six transfers.

The Pioneers are predicted to have a big year after AHA men’s head coaches voted them to top the conference standings in a preseason poll. Starting goaltender Ajeet Gundarah was also voted the Preseason Player of the Year.

title: Preview | Penn State field hockey looks ahead to a road weekend against Michigan State and Kent State
author: Annie Gleba | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State is going into the weekend with two back-to-back away games and on a three-game winning skid.

The Nittany Lions sit at a 6-4 record with a 1-1 conference record. So far this season, they are 2-1 on the road, with their only loss coming to No. 18 Monmouth.

First, the blue and white will face Michigan State on Friday before traveling to Ohio for its second match of the weekend against Kent State.

Michigan State

Michigan State currently sits at 4-7 with a 0-4 conference record. It hasn’t been able to beat a ranked opponent yet, taking notable losses to Northwestern, Indiana, Iowa, Michigan and Miami (Ohio). And the team hasn’t been able to win at home with a 0-5 record at Ralph Young Field.

The Spartans' best offensive player is Bianca Pizano, a senior forward who has spent all three years of her athletic career with Michigan State. Within the Spartans, she’s scored the most goals with a total of five and has collected 11 points. Her shots-on-goal percentage is 0.619 and she has started and played through all 11 games.

Pizano ranks No.17 in the Big Ten for overall shots with an average of 1.91 per game, No.11 for overall goals with an average of .455 per game and tied for second in the conference in game-winning goals with 2.

Michigan State’s offense relies heavily on Pizano to create scoring opportunities for the Spartans. Other notable offensive players include Lilian Knorr and Ellie Kendall.

Knorr is a junior who has the second-highest playing time with 508 minutes, achieving eight points and having a shots-on-goal percentage of 0.692. Kendall has a total of seven points with a shots-on-goal percentage of 0.750.

Defensively, the Spartans have two goalies who have traded the net back and forth. Lola Munoz de Verger has started six games, but has played in all 11. She has allowed 17 goals but stopped 32, for a 0.653 save percentage.

Catherine Wolf, Michigan State's second goalie, has started five games, allowed 12 goals and collected 29 saves. Wolf’s save percentage is 0.707, bringing the two goalkeepers' combined save percentage to 0.678.

On the Penn State side, Aby Deverka has only allowed 14 goals this season and has 42 saves with a save percentage of 0.750. She ranks No. 4 in goals-against average and shutouts per game in the Big Ten. Deverka is also ranked No. 2 in saves per game overall in the Big Ten.

The two Big Ten teams will meet Friday at 3 p.m.

Kent State

After Friday's game, Penn State takes on Kent State at noon on Sunday. The Eagles sit at an overall record of 2-9 and are currently on a three-game losing streak.

On offense, the Eagles' breakout player is Eva Usoz. The midfielder has six goals and leads her team with 12 points. Kent State will also rely on Sophia Livingston and Adelaide Gagnon. The pair have a combined three goals and seven points.

For the Nittany Lions offense, Ella Gaitan has been able to make a big impact as she leads her team in points with 16. Gaitan has scored seven goals with two assists, taking a total of 39 shots. The forward ranks No.4 in average shots per game in the Big Ten and No. 7 in average goals per game.

Another key offensive player is Sienna Dunn, who has achieved 12 points and an outstanding 10 assists. Dunn leads the Big Ten in assists per game in the Big Ten. This offensive duo has been able to help Penn State win games this season and put up a strong contest in close games.

Kent State’s sole goal keeper is Michaela Skinner, a fifth-year transfer from Liberty University, where she played for four years. She’s allowed 29 goals this season and has saved 54. Her total save percentage is 0.651.

As Penn State heads into the weekend, it can make a big impact on its record if it’s able to keep offensive pressure up against both Michigan State and Kent State.

title: Penn State K Ryan Barker ‘like a goldfish,’ balances innate talent with mental fortitude
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Lance Frazier, assistant athletic director and Kennett High School’s head football coach, was in his office when a group of custodians hurriedly threw open the door. They told Frazier there was a kid draining 50-yard field goals in the middle of the summer.

Curious but skeptical, Frazier went to investigate. He heard the loud sound of a cleat striking pigskin and knew it was different from the average kick. When he saw the culprit was 6-foot-2, Frazier assumed he was headed off to college.

But he wasn’t. That young man was Ryan Barker, an eighth grader who asked his father for a kicking tee at Christmas. Barker revealed it was his first time ever kicking a football, and he’d be a freshman at Kennett the coming academic year. Frazier was overjoyed — the Blue Demons found themselves a superstar kicker.

“I immediately looked at the heavens,” Frazier told The Daily Collegian. “The football gods had finally blessed us with freakish talent. He's kicking like two or three balls, so I run in the locker room like, ‘Let me go get this kid some extra balls he can use.’”

About a week after meeting Frazier, Barker said he was “thrown into the fire” and was torn between two worlds: the gridiron and the soccer pitch.

Barker was an established soccer player, and he balanced academics with being a multi-sport varsity athlete for the majority of his high school career.

Most days, Barker came straight from soccer to catch the tail end of football practice, as Kennett saved special teams drills for last. Barker was socially behind in the locker room because of that, as he was still getting to know the team, according to Frazier.

“He was a typical kicker,” Frazier said. “They're a little bit off to the side, different from everybody in terms of how they prepare because their pressure is different from everybody else's.”

Frazier saw Barker’s potential and told him coaches such as Nick Saban and James Franklin were going to ask him, “Are you going to play soccer, or are you going to kick the football?”

Barker chose football ahead of his senior year of high school, and he later became the first Division I football player from Kennett when he committed to the Nittany Lions as a preferred walk-on in July 2022.

Frazier said Barker attending Penn State meant so much for the program, as it’s a university with many alumni in Kennett Square, a small suburb of Philadelphia. Now, Barker’s young brother, Shay, is a Division I kicker at Syracuse, and the siblings played one season together at Kennett.

“We never had been a heavily-recruited area,” Frazier said. “There's so many Penn State roots and alumni here in Kennett. It was surreal. I knew the impact it would have on others. He's a legendary guy for the kids because he let them know that guys from Kennett can make it big time.”

Barker redshirted in 2023 and initially lost the starting job to Sander Sahaydak in 2024 until Sahaydak went 2-for-5 on his field goal attempts through four weeks. So Franklin turned to Barker, and the former walk-on made his debut against UCLA, converting on both of his field goals and all three extra point attempts.

The next week, he rose to collegiate stardom at Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum. Penn State and USC were tied, 30-30, in overtime before Barker kicked the 36-yard game-winning field goal, the first for the Nittany Lions since Sam Ficken’s strike from the same distance against UCF in 2014.

“That’s all I’ve ever wanted to do, is to hit a game-winning kick,” Barker said after the game on Oct. 12, 2024. “It means a lot to me and my teammates. I’m just super proud of myself.”

Special teams coordinator Justin Lustig has instilled in Barker the “one shot, one kill” mentality throughout his time at Penn State.

Although the basis of the phrase is meant to keep the special teams unit focused solely on the kick in front of them, Barker said there’s specific nuances to it as a kicker and he can’t simply flush every kick regardless of the outcome.

“It's being able to weigh the importance of the fact that it’s ‘one shot, one kill,’” Barker said. “It allows you to hone in on the sole focus of trying to replicate that feeling of the ball contact. That's how I would describe it.”

It’s something Lustig has taught the entire special teams unit including punter Nathan Tiyce and long snapper Blaise Sokach-Minnick, and Barker has used it to keep his emotions in check. When a kick goes awry, Barker “flushes” it, which has helped him deal with high-pressure situations.

“Once I got that mindset going, the pressure was just non-existent, honestly, because it gave me a centered focus on what I needed to do,” Barker said Aug. 7. “The outside noise and pressure is something that could distract me if I let it. I'm not gonna let anything get in the way of what I need to do.”

With his talent and Lustig’s coaching, Barker has positively impacted his fellow special teamers. Tiyce serves as Barker’s holder, and he’s been inspired by his mental fortitude.

“He's one of the toughest people I know,” Tiyce said. “The way he rebounds and responds to adversity is his key to everything. He'll go on the sideline, and he's like a goldfish. The only thing we're focusing on is that next kick.”

Deep down, however, Barker intimately knows the stinging pain of a missed kick, but Frazier it’s a mental skill Barker’s built as he’s matured.

Barker’s had two misses so far this season, but he said those moments of failure are what motivate him to be better.

“You never want to have that feeling of what it feels like when you miss, and that's honestly the fuel that I use,” Barker said. “I hate the feeling of missing. It's really awful. So I’m chasing to never feel that again and it’s how I keep myself going.”

After falling to the Badgers, Barker said his role on the team is being a “safety net.” With the Nittany Lions 0-2 in the Big Ten, his ability to handle adversity is being tested much like how it was in 2025.

“If I go out onto the field, I'm putting points on the board when the offense may not be flowing as easily,” Barker said. “Embracing that as much as possible and knowing that I’ve got the team’s back — that's honestly where I want to be at.”

title: Staff predictions | What’s the outlook on Penn State men's hockey for the 2026-27 season?
author: The Daily Collegian men's hockey staff
description:
Penn State defenseman Jackson Smith sat hunched over in the visiting locker room of MVP Arena the night of March 27, already generating fuel for the 2026-27 season after losing to Minnesota-Duluth in the first round of the NCAA Tournament.

Over six months, 13 players lost to the professional level or graduation and an offseason used to try and make Smith’s last sentence true later, it’s officially game week again for the Nittany Lions, as they look for their third consecutive NCAA Tournament appearance.

“We wanted to win,” Smith said. “We wanted to win bad. But next year we're gonna remember this, and next year we're gonna win a (national championship).”

Can they play meaningful hockey in late March again? Here are our staff’s predictions for the 2026-27 season.

Chase Fisher: Falls short of NCAA Tournament bid

Penn State has 11 new roster additions, 12 if you count center Keaton Peters who was sidelined all of last year with an injury. So it’ll take time for the team to gel — and this was evident last season after going 10-7 in their first 17 games despite the loaded roster.

But unlike 2025, the Nittany Lions don’t have a non-conference schedule that can ease them into the year, give them time to build chemistry and let the new CHL players adjust to college hockey.

Two of the first three non-conference opponents are No. 16 UConn and No. 6 Quinnipiac, while they have to play six games, not eight like last year, before heading into Big Ten play. Not to mention the Big Ten competition is much better this season.

The preseason USCHO poll ranking of 17th for Penn State seems like it fits. The Nittany Lions will be a talented team, but after losing its top-four point scorers and five of its top six, it’s going to be tough to get into the dance in March.

Maggie Hardy: Falls short of NCAA Tournament bid

Penn State returns after falling short of last season's national championship hopes, ending with a much earlier-than-anticipated exit in the first round of the NCAA Tournament.

The Nittany Lions saw a significant roster overhaul in the offseason, losing five of their top six scorers, headlined by this year’s No. 1 overall NHL Draft pick Gavin McKenna. The program also has questions on the back end after losing both Jarod Crespo and Cade Christenson, two blueline staples.

The blue and white’s schedule looks to be an uphill battle, opening up with two ranked non-conference opponents in No. 16 UConn and No. 6 Quinnipiac. Conference play will be the true test for the program, as teams like Michigan, Michigan State and Wisconsin — all ranked within the preseason top-10 — are all predicted to have deep postseason runs.

Penn State still has the capabilities to put together a solid season, however, with Josh Fleming returning in net after a stellar freshman season, Smith anchoring the blueline as one of the best defenders in the conference, and some strong transfer portal additions like Maine forward Justin Poirier and Vermont defenseman Caeden Herrington.

Overall, with an almost entirely new roster and a gauntlet of a conference schedule, I predict Penn State will be neck-and-neck for one of the final NCAA Tournament bids, but will ultimately fall short and end its season in the Big Ten Tournament.

Dominic Megats: Falls short of NCAA Tournament bid

Penn State will struggle out of the gate, and there’s no way around it. That’s what comes with building a new team after losing several key players. However, the “high tempo” identity stays the same for coach Guy Gadowsky.

Forwards like Justin Poirier and Marco Mignosa will bring that style of play to the team, but at the same time they haven’t played in the Big Ten before.

Additionally, the Nittany Lions have no easy task when it comes to opening their season. They play two ranked opponents in their first three games: No. 16 UConn and No. 6 Quinnipiac. All in all, the blue and white will use six nonconference games to introduce its new faces to collegiate hockey before starting conference play.

Teams such as Michigan, Michigan State and Wisconsin will give Penn State a challenge it may not be able to conquer with the fresh forward group.

Gadowsky has a talented group of new players coming in; however, starting the season against ranked opponents followed by a difficult Big Ten gauntlet will prove to be too much for the young squad.

title: Penn State men’s soccer searches for breakthrough win against Michigan
author: Luci Palacios | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State men’s soccer looks to end a five-game losing streak on Friday when they travel to Michigan for another Big Ten Matchup.

The Nittany Lions are 2-7 overall and 0-5 in conference play this season. Both squads are looking for their first conference wins as Michigan enters at 3-4-2 and 0-2-1 in the Big Ten. Penn State has struggled on the road, going 0-3 this season.

Penn State leads the all-time series 16-12-5, with Michigan winning just once in the past six years. The teams played to a scoreless draw at Jeffrey Field on Nov. 7 last season. Michigan’s lone win during that stretch came on Sept. 13, 2024, when they defeated Penn State 2-1 at home.

Wolverines look to reset

Michigan is coming off a 2-1 loss to Portland on Sunday, their second loss in the last three games. Portland took control early, scoring twice in three minutes. The Pilots found the back of the net in the 18th and 21st minutes to take a 2-0 lead.

Michigan finally broke through with nine seconds left in the game. Freshman Alex Gimple scored his first career goal, with Nico Pendleton and Kian Concepcion getting assists.

The late goal gave the Wolverines a chance, but they didn’t have enough time to find an equalizer.

Grayson Elmquist has been the Wolverines’ top scorer this season with four goals, putting him in the top-10 in goals scored in the Big Ten.

Pendleton and Joao Paulo Ramos have each recorded three assists to lead Michigan in that category.

Alen Bean has started all nine games in goal for the Wolverines. He’s made 20 saves and allowed 11 goals, giving him a .645 save percentage, ranking eighth in the Big Ten.

Michigan will try to put Sunday’s loss behind them against a Penn State team that’s struggling to find their footing in conference play.

Nittany Lions chase a breakthrough

Penn State put up a battle against Ohio State this past Friday.

The Nittany Lions held a 1-0 lead against the Buckeyes for a majority of the game until Ohio State scored twice in the final three minutes, coming away with a 2-1 win.

The blue and white got on the board in the 33rd minute when Grant McIntosh won the ball on a corner kick and found Joe Sheridan in the 18-yard box, setting up Etienne Reck for the finish.

Reck had one of his better games of the season, taking a career-high five shots and scoring his third collegiate goal. The Nittany Lions finished with 14 shots, the highest total of the season, and had 10 shots on target before halftime.

They couldn’t quite hold onto the lead as Ohio State tied the game off a corner kick with less than three minutes remaining. Then, with just nine seconds left on the clock, the Buckeyes found the game-winner. Junior defender Martin Wurschmidt scored both goals, giving him his third and fourth goals of the season.

Daniel Peluffo-Wiese has been busy in goal during Penn State’s recent stretch. He’s made 28 saves this season and owns a .583 save percentage. His 3.11 saves per game rank fourth in the Big Ten.

Friday’s game carries another layer of significance for Penn State, as coach Rob Dow is still looking for his first Big Ten win.

With both teams coming off losses, Penn State has a chance to change the direction of their season and rebuild against a familiar opponent. A win in Ann Arbor would end the Nittany Lions’ five-game losing streak and add a meaningful win as they head into the rest of the season.

title: Column | ‘The Scarlet Letter’ proves shame keeps us from living
author: Kippi Hall | The Daily Collegian
description:
No one dances in the club anymore.

The club, or the State College equivalent, remains a place to bob up and down in a crowd without being too obvious or overeager to move, especially without looking weird. The threat of being found imperfect lives in the flash shining from someone recording on Snapchat for their private story.

The threat of public ridicule continues when the lights turn back on, too. Like the Puritans of 17th-century Boston in Nathaniel Hawthorne’s “The Scarlet Letter,” the looming cloud of potential shame makes us dampen our efforts to experience life properly because making a mistake is a mortal sin in 2026.

“The Scarlet Letter,” published in 1850, chronicles the journey of a woman named Hester Prynne (which intentionally rhymes with “sin,” per my AP English Language and Composition teacher) who commits adultery and bears the child out of wedlock, then slated to wear a bright red “A” that stands for “adultery” on her chest for life.

Who did she do it with? The pastor and most pious man in the village, Arthur Dimmesdale.

However, no one in the town knows the identity of the father and Hester swears herself to secrecy, bearing the brunt of criticism from society.

The townspeople, as soon as she exits the prison, begin gossiping about Hester’s sin and how she should be punished, but not without Hawthorne highlighting their own flaws: “‘What do we talk of marks and brands, whether on the bodice of her gown, or the flesh of her forehead?’ cried another female, the ugliest as well as the most pitiless of these self-constituted judges. ‘This woman has brought shame upon us all, and ought to die.’”

Judgment levied against other people is so common that there are major Bible passages warning against it. We dislike what a person’s wearing, how they speak, what they do on a daily basis and choose to treat them differently based on our judgements when we often exhibit those exact traits ourselves.

The fundamental attribution error, a common psychological bias in humans, pushes us to attribute mistakes to a moral deficiency or personal failure in others, even though those same mistakes are due to factors out of our control when we’re in the wrong.

The “ugly, self-constituted judges” in the novel want to eradicate Hester’s blemish on the history of their town with even village’s leader, Gov. Bellingham, proposing that Hester’s illegitimate child, Pearl, be taken from her as Hester’s sin made her unfit to be a mother. The same leader preaching spirituality also lives lavishly throughout the course of the novel, directly opposing the ideals of the religion the Puritans follow.

There is such a thing as healthy judgment, since it is such a critical part of the way we navigate the world. Sometimes an instinctual “ick” allows us to avoid dangerous or otherwise unpleasant situations. But when we ignore the lines of thinking that would offer compassion to others and instead choose to die on a hill based on a single act, we become the self-constituted judges that we fear so much.

The internet acts as the townspeople and the scarlet letter on Hester’s bodice. While marks of the same mistake live on forever in the digital world like an ink stain, that same community ridicules and relentlessly ostracizes the one with the mark. In doing so, we deprive ourselves the opportunity to make mistakes and truly live.

Hester has the opportunity to leave Boston village and shed her sin to begin a new life. But she stays and faces the music, because the scarlet letter is proof she did something out of passion and love.

Dimmesdale, however, avoids confession and the Puritans of the town continue to regard him as a perfect, devout man, even attributing his visible inner turmoil to his holiness. The pastor physically and emotionally deteriorates as his secret sin and internal passion for Hester burn through his facade, a remarkably similar fate for when we try to subdue our own desires to experience life fully.

Going out and socializing with the fear of making a fool of ourselves or trying a new hobby we aren’t immediately good at, like dancing at the club, are some of the greatest tools we have against depression. Conversely, social and physical inactivity are greatly associated with higher risks of depression, according to a study published in the National Institute of Medicine. Psychological biases like the spotlight effect in concert with the omnipresent chance of being shamed online make those activities that much more difficult to do, because the constant judgment is proof that any mistakes are the whole constitution of who we are.

But Hester Prynne disagrees. Her past makes her a resource for compassion for the townspeople, morphing the scarlet letter into a symbol of owning who you are regardless of what others believe and being empathetic to those who try and fail, too.

Mistakes are an inevitable part of who we are and to get rid of them or attempt to explain them away would be disingenuous. However, they’re not our entire character and, wrong or not, they paint the background of who we choose to be beyond them.

The narrator states, “If truth were everywhere to be shown, a scarlet letter would blaze forth on many a bosom.” The ubiquity of our flaws makes judgment, outward and inward, seem ridiculous, and turns the nightmare of failing in front of others into nothing more than a bad dream to move on from.

Shame is a powerful force that can be wielded unfairly and excessively, leaving us paralyzed and projecting that guilt onto those who put our flaws on display. But puritanical standards don’t align with having a full life.

We all need to dance at the club some more, stopping only to admire those who trip over their own ankles then rebalance themselves to continue doing it anyway.

title: Preview | No. 4 Penn State women’s hockey travels to face Syracuse in first road series
author: Aeryn Ajot | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions are on a winning streak. With that momentum, its upcoming matchup against Syracuse will be a first road test to see if the dominant players Penn State has brought in will continue this winning turnaround.

Will the blue and white win in Orange territory, or will they take another loss to their 2-2 record in Atlantic Hockey American (AHA) play?

Series history

This week, the Nittany Lions play against the Syracuse Orange on Friday and Saturday. In the past, Penn State would’ve had a run for its money, but in recent years and with star players, the story’s been a bit different.

Penn State has struggled against Syracuse, with a 12-38-8 record in games all time. In the past two years, however, the blue and white has faced the Orange four times and won each time, with the largest margin being 11-2 in their November 2025 matchup.

This upcoming game will make another point about the Penn State women’s hockey team and how its season will look after a Frozen Four finish last year.

Scouting Syracuse

Similar to Penn State, Syracuse hasn’t had a perfect season either, with a 3-1 overall record and a 1-1 conference record.

Syracuse started with a strong 2-0 home winning streak against Stonehill but lost it in the second game, 5-2 against Mercyhurst. Although strong in their first three games, the Orange have now lost momentum and are playing the blue and white on an even playing field.

Previous teams Syracuse have played this season have been unranked and far less competitive than the teams that Penn State has faced. Both Stonehill and Mercyhurst were unranked and put up a good fight against Syracuse, with the Orange's largest victory margin being three points.

2026 Penn State season

After a successful season, Penn State is ranked at No. 4 in the USCHO D1 Poll, behind Wisconsin, Ohio State and Minnesota. It earned this spot after a huge demonstration of talent at the AHA Tournament, where the Nittany Lions beat No. 12 Mercyhurst for the second year in a row and brought home the fourth consecutive conference title.

In the past few weeks, Penn State hasn’t reflected last year's Frozen Four finish very well. Earning a 2-2 record, it looks at face value that coach Jeff Kampersal’s squad is having a hard start to the season; however, when looking at the Nittany Lions’ opponents, it’s a different story.

Penn State, compared to Syracuse, fought No. 2 Ohio State, a worthy opponent and last year’s runner-up in the Frozen Four contest. Historically, Penn State has lost more than won against Ohio State, with a record of 2-13 as of this season. The Buckeyes’ dominant offense and aggressive defense has always been a challenge for the Nittany Lions, and that was the result again this season.

Compared to Syracuse, Penn State’s loss shows it remains a strong, consistent competitor, holding its own against the No. 2 team in the nation. At the same time, Syracuse continues to struggle against unranked teams.

title: Penn State men's soccer notebook | Rob Dow talks tactical preparation for match against Michigan
author: Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian
description:
After another tough loss this season to Ohio State left men’s soccer with a growing losing record, the Nittany Lions will look to break through in Ann Arbor this Friday.

Coach Rob Dow sat down to talk about the mentality going into this week’s match-up and what he thinks it’s going to take to get the team back on the saddle.

Here is what was discussed.

Learning from mistakes

It’s no secret that the blue and white have talent. The Nittany Lions consistently start the first half of play dominant and put pressure on the ball early. Yet, more often than not, they cannot seem to carry that fuel into the second, which is where many of their losses seem to come from.

“We wanted to approach this week of training to make sure our environment feels uncomfortable the entire time, and that’s illustrated by the coaches’ demands, but mostly from the leadership perspective, to execute from a higher level of intensity, followed by being an all-American at the basic things,” Dow said.

During the loss against Ohio State, the Nittany Lions struggled to remember the basics, with Dow mentioning a lack of marking on the Buckeyes players, being the team to get the second ball and bouncing back to re-organize on corners.

Mentality shift

Dow emphasized the team’s mantra of " all-American,” and how they are trying to bring that into every aspect of training.

“Early is on time,” Dow said. “Let’s go back to making sure that during our stretching time, we’re being all-American stretchers. From a sleep and nutrition standpoint, let’s get everything we need and prioritize that. We got eight hours of sleep, non-negotiable. ”

He also reflected on a comment made at the end of last week’s game, when he wanted the players to hear Ohio State cheering on Jeffrey Field, a game they should have won. While he was upset, he saw it as an opportunity to get comfortable with the uncomfortable.

Dow also believes that the best way to do this is to make sure that players are feeling okay off the field, to bring their best to the field.

“Peeling back the layers because we got to get right from a humanistic standpoint of making sure that we’re not boiling over and emotional going into the next game,” Dow said. “That we’re dialed in as real people and go back to the basics, to be the hardest team in the country while being the most tight, united family team environment.”

Play strategy

While players like Etienne Reck and Joe Sheridan have been key to making crucial moves in games, Dow wants to avoid relying too heavily on them to do all the work.

“We need to say zero goals on restarts,” Dow said. “We’re not necessarily not winning the first ball, but once it goes over or becomes over-reliant on Noah Forester, Joe Sheridan, Etienne Reck, just winning these balls, our players are just relying on them to do all the jobs,” Dow said.

The Wolverines have executed corners well throughout the season, hitting in the range and using crossing tactics to get numbers up in the attack and cross so wide. To prevent this, the Nittany Lions will focus on building their own pressure on both fronts to cut them off before they take up too much room in the box.

Michigan has a center back who is weak using his right foot, and is a key pressing trigger for this game.

“If we can get the ball to rise to his left foot, press from a jump on that side, build on the right, step up, and press,” Dow said. “hopefully go back into our pressure pocket high.”

title: Penn State offensive linemen share thoughts on struggles, practice changes
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s offensive line hasn’t played up to the standard it set for itself at the beginning of the season. The run game has struggled due to a combination of the line not opening wide enough gaps and individual blocking issues which have stalled the offense on numerous occasions.

The room had its worst performance of the season against Northwestern as the running backs only rushed for 48 yards on Friday.

Right guard Cooper Cousins was open about the room’s apparent shortcomings when he took the podium on Tuesday after the Wildcats handed the Nittany Lions their second-straight defeat. He noted the room needs to be better working together.

“Five need to work as one,” Cousins said. “It can't be one guy having a good block and four guys semi-doing their job. You’ve got to connect and click on all cylinders, no matter what's going on, no matter what looks out there against us, we just really have to execute our job with the highest capability possible.”

Cousins said a lot of it boils down to the offensive line’s execution of the playcalls. He made no excuses and didn’t point fingers, saying how it doesn’t matter if it’s a run or pass play, the five linemen have to be on point to carve a path for the offense.

The struggles in the run game have been especially frustrating for the Nittany Lions, and Cousins said it’s “every offensive lineman’s dream to run the ball and have success in the run game.”

Cousins and right tackle Anthony Donkoh voiced their optimism about how this week at practice has gone and feels the unit is growing forward, crediting the coaching staff for their guidance.

Additionally, Donkoh said the coaching staff has reflected on the struggles in the run game and have made adjustments in practice to address flaws they’ve recognized. He noted how the offensive line is working on understanding the “intent” of run plays.

“We just have to play with five as one — it's that simple,” Cousins said. “That's ultimately what we have to do, so we can get (the running backs) the glory that they deserve and everything that they've been working for. That's when it's going to come to fruition, and we'll spring those runs.”

Donkoh said the growth will come from being in situations at practice where they’re “forced to communicate.” Such situations include defensive presnap motion, to which the line uses center Brock Riker as a conduit for communication across the offensive line when quick adjustments are required.

“The biggest thing is anytime we bring edge pressure or pressure inside the box, we have to talk and have our eyes up to be able to see everything,” Donkoh said Wednesday. “And have trust that the person next to us is going to be able to do his job and pick up whoever's coming off the edge or in the box. Practice is what helps out with that, and that's how we get better with us moving as one.”

Both Cousins and Donkoh are confident in their fellow linemen. Looking ahead to USC, there’s a lot of uncertainty, but the offensive line will once again look to get the offense rolling in Big Ten action.

“We know the type of guys that we have in that room,” Cousins said. “We know the depth that we have in that room, and we know our capabilities in that room. We just need to have conviction, which we've seen at times.”

title: Penn State women's basketball notebook | Coach Tanisha Wright talks identity, program building
author: Lucas Yendrzeiwski | The Daily Collegian
description:
With the Lady Lions set to tipoff their season in 26 days, Tanisha Wright returned to Chicago.

The first-year coach returned to the city where she most recently coached before heading to Happy Valley, holding history with the Chicago Sky. Wright was in the Windy City for other reasons: to participate in Big Ten Women’s Basketball Media Day on Wednesday. She laid out what fans can expect to see from the team in her first season at the helm and more.

Here’s a recap of Penn State’s participation in conference media day, streamed on the Big Ten Network.

Introducing a new era

Wright had the unique challenge of having to bring in an entirely new roster after 10 Lady Lions hit the transfer portal following the firing of long-time coach Carolyn Kieger.

“For me, number one was getting some players, because I had zero players,” Wright said.

Wright brought seven players from the transfer portal, and complemented them with a three-member incoming freshman class.

Now that the team is in place, Wright has shifted her focus to getting the team playing the Lady Lion brand of basketball, which Wright defined as “playing hard, playing smart, being competitive and understanding that we have to play together.”

Junior guard Devyn Quigley, an incoming transfer from NC State, is confident that the team is accepting coach Wright’s philosophy and coming together as a unit.

“You can’t even tell that we’re a new team,” Quigley said. “We literally love being around each other.”

Employing a pro mentality

With all of Wright’s coaching experience coming at the WNBA level, highlighted by a three-year stint as the coach of the Atlanta Dream from 2021-2024, she plans to bring a similar approach to how she runs her team at the collegiate level.

“I want to treat them like they’re pros,” Wright said. “Understanding that even though we’re still in college, there’s some similarities that they can have, like how they approach the game.”

Wright noted that playing at the professional level can be similar to the attention the Big Ten receives from fans and the media. Expectations are high after UCLA won the national championship last April and seven other conference members made the final AP Top 25 poll.

“(The) Big Ten is the best conference in the country, and so this is a huge stage to play on,” Wright said. “As a pro, you’re always playing on a huge stage, so I think there are similarities that I can bring to the table for sure.”

Wright is confident that the lessons she has learned throughout her professional journey both as a player and coach will help prepare her team as conference foes push them to play fast and in transition.

“I’ve been around Hall of Fame coaches, Hall of Fame players that have really poured into me as a coach,” Wright said. “So being able to teach all the things that I’ve learned throughout my journey of basketball is what I want to do with our players.”

Building a staff

Wright set the tone of building Lady Lion culture as she constructed her staff in April, including her former teammate Kelly Mazzante. Another addition to the staff with ties to program roots is graduate assistant Nevaeh Tot, daughter of Helen Darling, who played for the Lady Lions from 1996-2000.

“I think you have to have a great understanding of what Penn State is and what Penn State isn’t,” Wright said. “So bringing back people who understood what it was and what it is was really, really important.”

Wright also elaborated on what she felt Penn State is and what she hopes these staff additions can help communicate to her players.

“It’s a feeling, right? It’s an aura that they can just share from their lived experience,” Wright said.

title: Penn State women’s volleyball notebook | Coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley discusses past week, upcoming slate
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
A big weekend awaits Penn State.

The Nittany Lions return to the court this week after a split result over two matches: a sweep against No. 1 Nebraska and a four-set victory over Iowa. Coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley’s unit slipped to No. 18, a two-spot bump, following the result, as the blue and white resume its homestand at Rec Hall with a pair of Big Ten clashes.

With Northwestern arriving in Happy Valley on Friday and No. 20 Washington on Sunday, Schumacher-Cawley held weekly media availability on Wednesday. Here’s a recap of those remarks.

Wild week

After the two matches for Penn State couldn’t have gone any more differently, as the Cornhuskers cruised to a result where the blue and white failed to match the visiting foe’s attacking prowess.

“I think the team is responding well,” Schumacher-Cawley said. “Coming up with two matches at home, and you got to win at home, so I think being prepared and getting a good week of practice in is going to set us up for success.”

The Nittany Lions’ coach also revealed the intention in those practices, as in both games this weekend, the blue and white dropped its opening sets in narrow fashion.

“That has been the key this week in practice: being able to start quicker,” Schumacher-Cawley said. “Unfortunately, we've had way too many errors, and until we settle in, the focus at the start is gonna be a little bit different.”

Player personnel

The Nittany Lions, more than ever this season, embody the mantra of ‘strength in numbers,’ as they have frequently rotated personnel with its incredibly young roster littered with marquee freshmen.

“I think we've learned a lot so far in the season, and I think that I think the team is getting better, and that's the goal,” Schumacher-Cawley said. “Every time we step on the floor, to be a better team, we're trying just to get the best out of each position we can right now.”

In both of its games last week, Iowa and Nebraska only deployed 10 players throughout the match’s duration, while the blue and white substituted 12 and 14, respectively, over both games. The blue and white have also been without star middle blocker Ryla Jones, who was on crutches with an apparent lower-body injury, as the rotation has been utilized to fill that gap.

Schumacher-Cawley gave props to freshman middle blocker Kendall Northern, who has been filling in for Jones, but also said the primary starter in the position should be back “in a couple of weeks.”

The Penn State boss also gave props to setter Alexis Stucky, who had a season-high 54 assists in Iowa, praising the redshirt senior's offense and defense. That wasn’t all of Schumacher-Cawley’s positivity toward her players; she continued with positivity toward outside hitter Haley when questioned on her role, stating how the freshman proved her ability so far this season.

Yet when asked how the rotation shapes up in the outside hitter position group, the coach maintained that none has an upper hand as of now.

“I think they each have a different skill set that can help us, whether it's passing or being a better blocker and attacker,” Schumacher-Cawley said. “We'll need different things in that position every match, and so I know that they're ready to go.”

Development in the sport

With the ranked clash Thursday against the top-of-the-nation Cornhuskers, Nittany Lions fans came in full force in an attempt to drown out the sea of red that had traveled with Nebraska. The total attendance for the match at Rec Hall stood at 5,450, which carried the blue and white to a total attendance north of 9,000 for the week.

“What this sport means to Penn State and to not only the players here now, but everyone that came before them and the ones that will be coming here is really special,” Schumacher-Cawley said. “During preseason, all of the crazy tournaments we were in, we had several alums along the way, and I think just having them around and the support is really special, and I think our players understand that.”

Thursday was the boiling point of what has been a historic season for the blue and white in the spotlight. The aforementioned preseason saw the Nittany Lions compete at the Spikes Under the Lights tournament in the Dallas Cowboys’ AT&T Stadium. The blue and white also headed to Philadelphia’s Palestra and Chicago’s Wrigley Field, home of the Cubs. Yet with the spotlight still gleaming, Schumacher-Cawley has ideas for the future.

“I would say this preseason was, I don't know how we top that; maybe we get to Madison Square Garden and somewhere out here on the East Coast would be cool.”

title: Penn State newcomers ready for ‘once-in-a-lifetime’ White Out debut
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s White Out game has delivered some of the most memorable moments in college football and has recorded some of the biggest attendances in Beaver Stadium over the last 20 years.

While the Nittany Lions are coming off a two-game losing streak ahead of this week’s White Out against USC — making for one of the more unusual buildups to the spectacle in recent years — many of the new players are excited to take part in it for the first time.

“To see the crowd, see how loud they get, and feed off that energy, it’s going to be a cool experience,” tight end Benjamin Brahmer said Wednesday. “It’s a once-in-a-lifetime experience for me, so I’m excited.”

The game will be unfamiliar territory for a majority of Penn State’s starters, many of whom have come from Iowa State and haven’t seen anything like it. However, the Nittany Lions also have more than 50 returning players who’ve given the newcomers a glimpse of what to expect.

Brahmer said teammates have described the atmosphere as “surreal” and compared stepping onto the field to being in a movie.

“I’m juiced to get out there and feed off that energy from the crowd,” Brahmer said.

Offensive lineman Anthony Donkoh is one of the few returning starters for Penn State and will take the field for his fourth White Out game, having been on both sides of the result in the big game.

But even after playing in one of the most anticipated White Outs in recent years against Oregon last season, the game continues to be one of Donkoh’s favorite moments of the year.

“I told them, when we run out of the tunnel, soak it all in,” Donkoh said. “It’s going to be a movie scene out there. It’s definitely one of the coolest things that I’ve ever been a part of.”

Despite the hype around one of the greatest shows in college sports, Donkoh emphasized being cautious about becoming too consumed by the spectacle.

“Embrace it and lean into it when there’s opportunities to lean into it, but don’t get caught up in that,” Donkoh said. “At the end of the day, we’re there to play football and play at the highest level.”

Kicker Ryan Barker, who has also played in multiple White Outs, echoed his sentiment.

With the White Out comes added attention and excitement surrounding the program, especially considering the results over the last two weeks. For players going through this week for the first time, Barker said keeping that attention from becoming a distraction will be important.

“I think the most important thing is just eliminating the distractions,” Barker said. “A lot of guys will be experiencing that for the first time. So that’s kind of just been my message to all of the guys who are experiencing this for the first time, just keep the main thing the main thing.”

Matt Campbell is also taking part in his first White Out, but his role goes beyond just coaching from the sidelines, as he’ll welcome in loads of recruits during the biggest recruiting weekends during the season.

“It’s such an unbelievable opportunity to showcase this community and showcase the fan support, the community, what this place means, and how special it is to play football here at Penn State,” Campbell said. “It continues to showcase how special it is to play here at Penn State.”

As Penn State welcomes USC to Happy Valley at 7:30 p.m. Saturday, there will be plenty at stake. Campbell and his staff will have an opportunity to impress recruits, while the Nittany Lions will try to snap a two-game losing streak and avoid dropping three straight to start Big Ten play.

But Saturday will also provide Penn State an opportunity to reconnect with a fanbase that has watched the season take a sharp turn over the last two weeks. Even amid the recent struggles, Donkoh said having the fans still pack the stands would show their belief in the program hasn’t wavered.

“It would mean that the fans still care about us, still love us, still give us our support,” Donkoh said. “I know the defense especially feeds into that, feeds into the crowd pouring into them. I look forward to it a lot, and it’s gonna be fun. It always is.”
