title: Penn State women's hockey notebook | Jeff Kampersal speaks on playing without stars, Syracuse series
author: Mashiah Mitchell | The Daily Collegian
description:
After two massive series that have the Nittany Lions at 2-2 and atop the AHA standings as the only team undefeated in conference play, Penn State will head north to meet the Syracuse Orange in a two-game conference battle.

Before that, though, coach Jeff Kampersal spoke to the media ahead of his 20th series against the Orange in his Penn State coaching tenure.

Kampersal took questions regarding his plans for an offense that will be without two of its most dependable players, the biggest noticeable differences for the Orange this year compared to last season, and what his team carries into this series after two battles against Robert Morris.

Here’s a recap of the media availability.

Down two

In this series, the blue and white will be without star junior forwards Grace Outwater and Abby Stonehouse, as they were chosen for Team Canada’s selection camp to possibly make the roster for the IHF Women’s World Championship in November.

This is a big blow to the Nittany Lion offense, with Stonehouse and Outwater accounting for over 30 percent of the team’s total points so far this season.

Kampersal expects those who’ll be with the team to not only step up, but also show out. He says the game plan will be adjusted to feature freshman forwards like Kylie Amelkovich and Sofia Ismael as they come into their own.

“It will be different, of course, with the number of forwards; we lost a few last year during the Olympics," Kampersal said. "So we’re going to go in there with ten forwards, and people will fill those roles left by (Grace) Outwater and (Abby) Stonehouse. No matter how many we play with, we are confident in that number and ready to compete.”

Clementine vs. Orange

This year’s Syracuse team covered their graduation losses and plugged similar talent into those spots, including freshman defender Maryn Broderick, who replaces the towering Charlotte Hallet, a six-foot-tall cornerstone of the Orange’s past four seasons who recorded over 100 blocks in her 136 games played.

The Orange currently sit at 3-1 on the season, their best start up to this point in over ten seasons. Under the tutelage of former USCHO Coach of the Year Brian Idalski, Syracuse looks primed to return to the NCAA tournament, a feat the Orange has achieved only twice since the program’s inception.

Kampersall and his staff know the talent Syracuse has, and they plan to fight fire with fire in terms of taking advantage of the opportunities they open up with speed and puck control on the attack.

“They did add more speed with Kenny (Kendra Raypholtz) and more sizeable defenders who can get their body in the way," Kampersal said. "They work incredibly hard on the forecheck and are a defensively sound team, so we hope to catch them in transition to not hit that wall around the net they tend to create. Player-wise, it is very similar, just with more depth, size and speed.”

Battle of attrition

Penn State followed up two heartbreaking losses against the Ohio State Buckeyes with two massive wins against RMU. Throughout both series, the blue and white showed a never-say-die attitude, battling period after period as if the game was 0-0 from start to finish.

In the Robert Morris series specifically, they went down 0-2 in the first game, but came out in the third period and looked like a completely different team with a fresh set of skates.

Kampersal feels this was much needed for a team that is still integrating its new talent and seeing where they are both physically and mentally when the game may feel as if it is out of reach.

“Being more intentional with what we’re doing was a good message we got, especially that first game (against Robert Morris) when we went down 0-2," Kampersal said. "This group has a lot of grit & pride. Syracuse has a new coach; they’re quick, fast, so we’re gonna have to adjust to their speed, but the biggest thing we wanna carry into that series and forward is that we’re gonna battle to the end.”

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell calls for consistency, rhythm moving forward
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Matt Campbell met with the media Wednesday ahead of his first White Out as Penn State’s coach.

Ahead of the 7:30 p.m. kickoff against USC on Saturday, Campbell discussed his offensive line pieces, the consistency of the pass rush and finding the rhythm of the game in all aspects.

Here’s what Campbell had to say.

Offensive line cornerstones

Penn State’s offensive line struggled against Northwestern, but the youth of the unit gives Campbell hope for the rest of the season and the future.

Center Brock Riker is still battling through an injury and “is not 100%,” but is “a lot closer this week than he's been probably the last couple weeks.”

“We have complete faith in Brock, and he has been gutting it out, to be honest with you, the last couple of weeks,” Campbell said. “ I do think he has been, probably taking care of him in the last quarter, getting an extra day, I think he's certainly been a lot better.”

Campbell said Riker is a cornerstone offensive lineman for Penn State despite only being a redshirt sophomore. Alongside Riker, Campbell was also asked about left tackle Malachi Goodman.

Goodman is starting this season for the first time in his career after entering Penn State last year as a high 4-star recruit and the No. 56 player in the 2025 class.

“I think the one thing I do appreciate about Malachi, every week you've seen him get better and better and better, and I think that guy's going to be a cornerstone for us for the future for sure,” Campbell said.

Pass rush consistency

The pass rush has been inconsistent throughout the first five games, totaling seven sacks. Among those, Yvan Kemajou and Caleb Bacon are the only edge rushers to record a sack.

Linebacker Tony Rojas leads the team in sacks with three, so Campbell wants to see more from his edge rushers and pass rush as a whole.

“It goes back to the consistency and rhythm,” Campbell said. “When you're playing on second-and-2, it's hard to play good pass rush.”

Campbell has seen production from edge rusher Alex McPherson, who made his first start of the season against Northwestern. Despite not recording a sack, McPherson has a tackle for loss and nine tackles this year

“I'd say the great thing that I love about Alex is that consistency that we're talking about,” Campbell said. “He has showcased that in five weeks that he's played. He's played really good football. He's been physical at the point of attack. He's had the ability to create some one-on-one pass rush on first and second down, which I think that's hard to do.”

Finding rhythm

A big talking point from Campbell over the past two weeks has been the team’s inability to find the rhythm of the game.

Penn State has struggled to move the ball offensively, while also letting the opposing offenses find a rhythm to put points on the board.

“I think when you talk rhythm and flow, that's all three units,” Campbell said. “In the last six quarters, we have failed to play in rhythm as a football team.”

Against a team like USC, Campbell emphasized the need to find the rhythm of the game in all facets. The Trojans rank No. 29 in offensive scoring, averaging 37.3 points per game and have shown an ability to find a rhythm on offense led by quarterback Jayden Maiava.

If Penn State wants to win Saturday, it’s going to have to find a rhythm and play good team football, according to Campbell.

“When you play a team as talented as this USC team coming in, you're gonna have to play great team football,” Campbell said. “We're gonna have to do a great job offensively, we have to do a great job defensively and special teams are going to have to be special on Saturday for us to be the team that we need to be and continue to grow ourselves forward.”

title: Sports Editors Weekly | What to make of Penn State women’s hockey’s split start
author: Myles Hannak & Gianna Dowling | Sports Editors
description:
Editor’s Note: Sports Editors Weekly is a dueling column written by Collegian Sports Editors Gianna Dowling and Myles Hannak. It aims to provide timely debate on Penn State sports performance and news each week.

Fresh off the first Frozen Four appearance in program history, which took place in Happy Valley, coach Jeff Kampersal’s squad returns to the ice for another year of anticipated action.

With heavy departures throughout its roster, Penn State staggered through two grueling losses against No. 2 Ohio State and a pair of high-scoring victories to open AHA conference play against Robert Morris.

With such drastic performances to start the year, what should be the expectations for Kampersal’s unit this season?

Gianna Dowling: It’ll be hard to fill the voids

There’s no doubt that the Nittany Lions are coming off of a season to remember, and were even rewarded with a top-five ranking to start the season.

However, last season’s squad featured eight seniors, the most of any class on the roster. This goes to show that many of the key pieces from last year's Frozen Four squad are gone, and making up for lost talent isn’t something that can be done overnight.

The biggest piece lost was former forward Tessa Janecke, the No. 3 overall pick in the 2026 PWHL draft. Janecke left Happy Valley with 201 points — the most by any men’s or women’s hockey player. Her 89 goals and 112 assists were also the most by any player in program history.

The blue and white also have a void to fill inside the cage, after losing former goalie Katie DeSa to graduation. DeSa was a two-time AHA Goaltender of the Year and her 25 career shutouts, 0.818 winning percentage and 1.43 goals against average are all program records.

Penn State had some flashes of light on who could be the next woman up in its first two series. Freshman forward Sofia Ismael recorded a hat trick in Game 2 against Robert Morris, and earned the assist on the other goal the team scored.

Filling the spot of starting goaltender has been the biggest question mark for Kampersal this season, with both sophomore Maddy Campbell and freshman Morgan Stickney. In the series against Ohio State, both netminders recorded 30-plus saves.

It’s fair to say that Kampersal has to give some time before finding a way to fill the voids of Janecke, DeSa and others from last year's class. However, it's not to say filling gaps won’t be able to happen; it’ll just take some time.

Myles Hannak: Regression, yet toward a promising future

The season started about as expected for the Nittany Lions, given their heavy turnover, as Penn State staggered against a team that’ll likely be a national contender and beat up on a frequent conference foe.

The blue and white can lay claim to their four straight AHA titles, but that feat doesn’t look as easy to repeat this year. Kampersal’s unit has a roster with top-of-the-conference talent in Grace Outwater and a young core that seems to have the talent to win games, but it feels like the experience isn’t adequate to navigate a conference that’s beginning to catch up to those on the ice in Happy Valley while most of Penn State is still in the midst of its debut campaigns.

The defense appears thin, evident by the massive number of shots faced by Penn State in both series so far this year. While the offensive ranks are talented and deep enough to win games, a lot of those players are still wet behind the ears; it’s possible that veteran blueliners possess the capabilities to shut them down or that form doesn’t click at the same time toward a run at a championship.

It’s still early in the year and Penn State hasn’t shown signs of being streaky or cooling off, but another Frozen Four appearance feels like a tall task given the amount of growth needed for this group. Losing the AHA crown is a genuine possibility and it feels like the perfect dose of bulletin board material needed to inspire the program to get over the hump to bring home its first national title.

Happy Valley has been in a cycle of being close but not close enough to win a title; this group looks like it may have that future in its cards. Fans appear to be witnessing a season of hard growth and ignition toward that goal on the ice right now, but it is exactly what to want with where things are headed.

title: Penn State men’s hockey looks to fill gaps in forward group
author: Dominic Megats I The Daily Collegian
description:
In what felt like a season they had to win it all, the Nittany Lions lost in the opening round of the NCAA tournament to Minnesota-Duluth. This wouldn’t be the only loss headed Penn State’s way.

Several core players departed from the talented forward group — Gavin McKenna, most notably, and three teammates who played on the same line for most of the year.

However, with captains Reese Laubach, Dane Dowiak and others returning, Guy Gadowsky used the offseason to welcome in many new faces to his forward group in hopes of filling the voids.

Newcomers

Headlining the recent additions is Justin Poirier, a Valleyfield, Quebec, native who is one of three transfers.

Poirier played 27 games with Maine as a freshman before joining the Nittany Lions. Before playing collegiate hockey, the sophomore earned 80 points through 58 games in his most recent season in the QMJHL.

Poirier is a shoot-first player who is always searching for the back of the net. The winger brings a heavy shot and flourishes off the one-timer.

Staying in the QMJHL, Justin Larose is set to join the squad. The Saint-Lazare, Quebec, native is fresh off an 88-point season captaining the Newfoundland Regiment. Larose is a playmaker who consistently draws attention from defenders and away from his teammates.

Marco Mignosa is another point-racking player who comes to Happy Valley from the OHL. The winger posted 89 points through 65 games in his second season as an assistant captain. He later finished the playoffs with 17 points in 10 games.

The Toronto native brings a speedy transition from defense to offense, making him a reliable target in the offensive zone for his teammates. Additionally, Mignosa is capable of playing on both special teams units.

Andrew Kuzma is set to make his return to Penn State after missing his entire first season due to recovery from heart surgery, never actually suiting up for the blue and white. The Fort Myers, Florida, native spent time in the OHL to prepare him to return to the team.

Kuzma played for two teams in the OHL and totaled 39 points in 69 total games. He will now look to return to his former team, where he will have holes to fill in the depth.

Returners

Laubach and Dowiak return to lead the Nittany Lions both on and off the ice. This is Dowiak’s second season as captain after his first was cut short due to a season-ending injury. The senior recorded 18 points in 27 games last season.

Laubach finished fifth on the team in scoring last season, behind four departing players.

Three sophomores will have the spotlight shone on them brighter this year after the departures.

Luke Misa is set to continue the larger role he stepped into last season due to Dowiak’s injury. In his freshman year, Misa recorded 19 points through 37 games, spending brief time on the top line with McKenna and Aiden Fink.

Additionally, Shea Van Olm looks to improve in his second year. The Calgary, Alberta, native is coming off a 12-point season, scoring nine goals in 33 games.

Along with Misa, Van Olm will look to continue his production from last season to his second year, as he may fit into a top-six role with several open spots.

Lev Katzin will continue to be a key depth player for the Nittany Lions. The Thornhill, Ontario, native is coming off a five-point season through 36 games. Although production wasn’t shown as much on the scoresheet, Katzin is always a ball of energy whenever he steps on the ice and looks to help his team through physicality.

Evident firepower was added to the forward group that lost a lot of it. Penn State will see how its new additions mold with key returners in the Ice Breaker Tournament on Friday before its first game at Pegula Ice Arena on Oct. 16 against No. 6 Quinnipiac.

title: TikTok is arguing about iced coffee, and who gets labeled professional
author: Ally Sons | The Daily Collegian
description:
If you’ve been on TikTok in the last few weeks, I’m sure you’ve seen the discourse around bringing an iced coffee to an interview. The debate online originally sparked from a video created by Caitlin Wehniainen. She provided tips and insight to people going out for job interviews, specifically targeted to a younger audience who may have less experience in that world.

She said that bringing an iced latte makes it seem like you see this interview as an item on your list of errands for that day. She further explained that it seems too “casual,” like you’re not taking the interview seriously. People in the comments argued that it shows good time management skills and, by leaving the iced coffee at home, it forces people “to pretend we aren’t human.”

This sparked a lot of discourse online, as she only specifically referenced iced coffee as unprofessional. The comments also said that this is an opportunity for her to check her bias, claiming that the association with iced coffee is rooted in being considered inherently feminine.

Viewers voiced concerns that Wehniainen's post, in which she emphasized that she was only concerned with iced coffee, read as misogynistic and unfair.

It raised a question for a lot of people online: Would there be the same stigma around a hot, black coffee?

Black coffee is a drink that has been given an inherently male association by people discussing this situation. What about black coffee makes it masculine? Is it that, for a lot of people, it doesn’t taste good, and that men are expected, by traditional, societal gender roles, to embrace discomfort in their everyday lives?

This conversation also crossed over into the expectations of formal business wear in the workplace and what is considered professional and unprofessional. Some social media users argued that men can find professional-wear easier and more conveniently than women can.

Some also commented that expected workplace uniforms are often suits, and women struggle to find suits that fit. Because of this, women are then expected to wear skirts, dresses and heels which can be uncomfortable. Even then, their outfits still sometimes get deemed “business casual.”

Furthermore, what colors are considered professional? Blue, black and gray certainly are. But colors like pink are considered unprofessional and distracting.

When you look up “women’s business attire” online you’re met with suggestions like Urban Outfitters and Connections, even though you see cropped button down shirts or mini pleated skirts on their websites.

The sexualization of women’s business clothing might seem small, but it all adds to the perception placed on women in the business world, marking them as "incompetent" based on their wardrobes, according to an article from Joe Navarro Forensics. According to Vogue, this sexualization of workplace outfits is more than the "office siren" trend we see online — it takes away from the seriousness and validity of women in their industries.

According to the comments, women are also expected to have their hair done and makeup on to look put together and professional, while men are simply not held to those same standards of appearance.

Another TikToker user, Anna Papalia, with close to 2 million followers, posted a video pointing out that Black people aren't bringing an iced coffee to an interview, due to there already being so many barriers to entry for people of color in the business world.

The unemployment rate for Black people in America is 5.5%, while it’s 3.3% for white people, according to the U.S Bureau of Labor Statistics. The disparity is present. The comments included a large number of people sharing their experiences at job interviews saying that they go so far as to straighten their hair or change their voice or dialects. They wrote that they worry about using their real names due to the risk of discrimination.

The business world is hard enough to break into, and finding interviews feels impossible to some. Is it just easier to comply to potentially flawed and arguably biased standards of professionalism, or is it worth it to be authentically yourself even with the risk of a negative reaction?

title: Recent Penn State alumni who got real on reality TV
author: Sarah Price | The Daily Collegian
description:
With a network of over 800,000 Penn State alumni, it’s fairly common to run into or spot another Nittany Lion while traveling, and sometimes, they can even be in your own home.

When you’re watching reality TV, of course.

As this genre of TV has become more popular over the past couple of decades, there are bound to be a few notable appearances from Penn State alumni — some of which have won their show, too.

Here are the most recent notable appearances from Penn State alumni in reality TV.

Love Island USA

Sincere Rhea, 25, of Cape May, New Jersey, and former Penn State track and field athlete, won the Big Ten 60-meter hurdles championship at Penn State in 2021. However, you probably don’t know him as a former Division I athlete.

Instead, Rhea has found fame in the pursuit of love on Season 8 of “Love Island USA," a reality TV show in which a group of singles move to an island in hopes of finding a connection.

Rhea entered the villa on day one and was coupled with Melanie Moreno, 24, of Philadelphia. Rhea and Moreno stayed a couple throughout the entire season, until viewers coupled Rhea with the new bombshell, Sol Dean, 24, from Orange County, California, on day 10 in the villa.

Drama ensued when the letter recoupling occurred just a few days later, where Rhea and Moreno chose to re-couple after writing love letters to each other, leaving Dean to couple with another islander who also didn’t receive a letter.

In a mid-season twist, Rhea, along with the other original males, were relocated to Casa Amor, where existing couples are separated and sent to different villas with new bombshells in order to test their loyalty.

Despite this twist, Rhea and Moreno remained a couple until their final date. Rhea came in third place alongside Moreno on the show.

Big Brother

Cam Sullivan-Brown, 27, of Bowie, Maryland, and former Penn State wide receiver, played under the lights of Beaver Stadium for five seasons from 2017 to 2021, before ultimately finishing his college career at the University of Massachusetts.

In 2024, Sullivan-Brown became a houseguest on “Big Brother” Season 26, a reality TV show in which a group of strangers are isolated in a house under constant camera surveillance, while competing in a series of social and physical challenges to avoid being evicted.

In a preseason interview for the show, Sullivan-Brown said he joined the “social experiment” because he knows how to talk to people, as the show is all about making friends. And it’s a competition after all, which seemed like an easy task for the former wide receiver.

On the show, Sullivan-Brown made numerous alliances with other houseguests, most notably with “The Pentagon” which included the winner of Season 26, Chelsie Baham, 29, of Rancho Cucamonga, California. However, Sullivan-Brown lost his key allies because of last-minute vote-flipping, which relegated him to the minority, which put Sullivan-Brown in a vulnerable position.

Despite this temporary set-back, Sullivan-Brown made a connection with Makensy Manbeck, 24, from Houston, which allowed him to coast through until the finale, where he was ultimately evicted by Manbeck. He placed third in the show.

Next Level Chef

Gabrielle Chappel, 32, of Jersey Shore, Pennsylvania, graduated from Penn State in 2016 with a degree in broadcast journalism and Spanish and has worked for companies like Fanatics as a digital producer and host. In 2021, Chappel experienced a career shift where she graduated from the Institute of Culinary Education's Health Supportive Culinary Arts program in New York City.

This career shift led Chappel to appear on Season 3 of “Next Level Chef,” a competitive reality cooking show with British celebrity chef, Gordan Ramsey as the creator and host. Nyesha Arrington and Richard Blais, American chefs and TV personalities, recruit contestants and serve as mentors, alongside Ramsey.

In the first three episodes of the season, contestants auditioned to be picked by one of the mentors – Chappel was chosen by Ramsey, alongside four other contestants. Chappel was the only chef from Team Ramsey to make it into the top three and enter the finale episode.

In the finale, each chef had 90 minutes to prepare a three-course meal as they moved through three kitchens, with the judges tasting their dishes immediately after preparation. Appetizers were first in the basement kitchen with Blais, and Chappel prepared pork meatballs with 67 minutes left in the challenge.

Next was a seafood course in the middle kitchen with Arrington where Chappel cooked a pan-roasted sea bream with a corn emulsion, roasted grapes and a fennel and radish salad. Finally, Chappel headed to the top kitchen with Ramsey, with a two-minute advantage to select anything she wanted and chose to cook a New York strip steak as her entree.

Chappel’s three-course meal won over the taste buds of the judges, which won her a grand prize of $250,000 and a one-year mentorship from each of the judges.

Beast Games

Tyler Lucas, 33, of Bellefonte, Pennsylvania, and former Penn State wide receiver, graduated from Penn State in 2015 with a degree in criminology. A year later, Lucas joined the United States Air Force as a cryptologic analyst and reporter and became a pilot in 2023.

Lucas made his reality TV debut on Season 1 of “The Titan Games,” an American sports competition series, hosted and created by Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson. Lucas ultimately lost before the finale.

However, it didn’t set him back from participating in another reality TV show in the future. Lucas joined “Beast Games,” a large competition series created by the famous YouTuber, Mr. Beast, as a contestant in Season 2: Strong vs. Smart.

The season began with 200 contestants, with Lucas being No. 167, as he competed in numerous challenges such as rope climbing, a dodgeball-style game, an obstacle course and many more that tested his abilities. The show even collaborated with the famous reality TV show, “Survivor,” for one of the challenges.

In the finale, Lucas competed against Cory Sims, 42, from Jamestown, New York, known as No. 191.

In the final challenge, each contestant took turns hiding a $5 million check in one of 10 briefcases, while the other was blindfolded. Then, the blindfolded player would remove their blindfold and try to guess which briefcase held the $5 million check.

After several stressful rounds, Lucas ultimately picked the correct suitcase to win the ultimate prize.

While suffering through final exams this semester, be thankful you’re not risking $5 million, cooking for Gordon Ramsey or being constantly recorded.

title: Penn State professor invents first autonomous Double Dutch machine
author: Anisa Daniel-Oniko | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State Professor Tahira Reid Smith’s Double Dutch machine began in the eighties with a poster and a dream.

At the time, Double Dutch was commonplace and popular, a hobby that involved two jump ropes moving in two different directions. It was dominated by women and Black girls, and it was the kind of game you couldn’t play alone. If you grew up in New York City, Chicago or Philadelphia, you played Double Dutch, Reid Smith said, and so too did anyone with a sidewalk on their street.

“It really goes back to a very old story,” Reid Smith, a mechanical engineering professor and founder of Jump Dreams, Inc., said. “There was some kind of poster contest for the whole third grade class, and we were asked to draw a picture of something we wish we could have in the future.”

Reid Smith wanted to play Double Dutch, but she was an only child, so she always had to wait to play at school. That’s why she drew a poster of an autonomous Double Dutch machine that would let her jump alone.

She won first prize, which her third-grade self found affirming, but didn’t think about the machine again until she was an undergraduate student at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI). Reid Smith, who had been part of a program RPI did to reach high schoolers, majored in engineering.

“I couldn't leave my block to go where people were,” Reid Smith said. “That's where that idea first started.”

Deborah Nazon, who was RPI’s Assistant Provost for Institute Diversity, sees Reid Smith as her “godbaby.” At the time, there weren’t many Black engineering majors at RPI. And Reid Smith “was amazing just walking in the door,” Nazon said; she could see her brilliance from the day she met her.

At RPI, Reid Smith took a required course called Introduction to Engineering Design. The theme that semester was challenging the limits in sports and recreational activities.

“I thought about the obvious sports — football, basketball,” Reid Smith said. “Then I was like, ‘Wait a minute, that idea I had in third grade, what about that?’”

As soon as the recollection dawned upon her, her notebook “went crazy,” with her ideas expanding in the midst of something she “could completely relate to.”

From then on, Reid Smith worked on several iterations of the prototype for her autonomous Double Dutch machine. Sometimes she would bring Nazon’s young son with her to the lab and let him watch her work — which inspired him to pursue and receive a PhD in mechanical engineering.

“I've seen (the machine) from when it was in the lab, when it was just a prototype of sorts,” Nazon said. “I'd stop in, my son would see it, he'd come home, he was very excited. And she kept at it.”

The first functional prototype was created in 2000. After that, there were “lots of fits and starts,” partly because Reid Smith was continuing her education and becoming a professor at the same time.

“There were times I tried to kind of go back to (the machine), but coming to Penn State has been pivotal,” she said. “It's been a real blessing, to be honest, to be here. Not just as a professor, but

being in a space where I was able to revisit this idea.”

Reid Smith’s newfound proximity to Philadelphia, New York City and development zones like Launchbox was “a gamechanger.” She returned to the machine, partnering with a product designer in California to create a version of it that winded up gaining traction online.

During the Launchbox IdeaTest Lab program last year, she met Renie Johnson, a Penn State alumna with over a decade of experience researching innovation for Corning Inc.

Two things about Jump Dreams stood out to Johnson: The first was that Reid Smith’s machine was the only piece of automated gym equipment more than one person could use at the same time. The second was the emotional advantage she spotted for Johnson’s product.

“With Double Dutch, especially in the urban community, it is such a tight, emotional connection to that product,” Johnson, who is now an analyst for Jump Dreams, said. “I got to go with her to Philly Jumps. To see the look — it was mostly women — but to see the look on their face, it's something so special.”

People from across the world, including the United States, Japan, Italy, France, Croatia and Argentina, have reached out to Reid Smith. A seven-time Double Dutch champion thanked her for her invention she said.

She’s done two events to showcase her machine, including the Philly Girl Jumps Double Dutch event that takes place every first Saturday in May for Double Dutch Day. The second event in State College gave jumpers an opportunity to give feedback on the machine.

“My goals are to release a product that is fully refined based on all the feedback from people who tried it out,” Reid Smith said.

Going forward, she plans to engage a wider user base of various kinds of athletes, launch a Kickstarter campaign to raise funds for manufacturing and put out another version that incorporates all new design changes. The hardest part is refining the hardware, she said, but Reid Smith and Johnson are optimistic that preorders will be available in February 2027.

There are hundreds of names on the waitlist.

“Honestly, I believe with all my heart this is going to be big,” Johnson said.

title: Puerto Rican Penn State students reflect on the island’s political status, future
author: Fabiola González-Cruz | The Daily Collegian
description:
The island of Puerto Rico became a U.S. territory 128 years ago, a governmental status that still remains today. As a territory, Puerto Rican citizens are classified as U.S. citizens and are protected under the Fourteenth Amendment and citizens are protected by fundamental civil rights.

This has led to debate on possible futures for the island, including statehood, independence, free association and maintaining the current territorial relationship. For Puerto Rican students, the question extends beyond political terminology and into questions of identity, representation, autonomy and Puerto Rico’s relationship with the U.S.

Ignacio Pedraza, 18, of Bayamón, Puerto Rico, said he favors maintaining Puerto Rico’s current political relationship with the U.S., pointing to the degree of autonomy the island maintains while also benefiting from its relationship with the U.S.

Pedraza, a first-year studying international politics, pointed to Puerto Rico’s ability to compete separately in the Olympic Games as something he sees as part of the island’s distinct identity. At the same time, he acknowledged problems within the current relationship, particularly Puerto Rico’s reliance on the U.S.

"I'm an athlete, and one of the things I most cherish about Puerto Rico is that we have our own Olympic Committee,” Pedraza said “If we become a state, we’d completely lose that.”

By the mid 20th century, Puerto Rico began gaining more authority over the administration of its own government. Puerto Ricans began electing their own governor in 1948, and Congress authorized the island to draft its own constitution in 1950. The constitution took effect in 1952, establishing the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, but it didn’t make Puerto Rico a state or an independent country.

Rather than seeing a change in political status as the solution to Puerto Rico’s problems, Pedraza said he believes stronger leadership could improve conditions under the current arrangement.

Gabriela López, 19, of Mayagüez, Puerto Rico, said her perspective on Puerto Rico’s political status began long before she was old enough to vote.

One of the first essays she remembers writing in grade school was on what she could change in the world, López, a second-year studying broadcast journalism, said. At around 8 years old, she chose Puerto Rican independence, despite growing up with parents who supported different political parties and did not openly discuss their political beliefs with her.

“We’re a part of the United States, but they never treat us like we’re theirs,” López said, recalling what she wrote in her essay.

Years later, López said Hurricane María shaped how she understood that relationship.

The Category 4 hurricane struck Puerto Rico on September 20, 2017, devastating the island’s electrical grid and other infrastructure. The U.S. Government Accountability Office later documented extensive delays and complications in long-term recovery projects.

“My mother hung Christmas lights on a tree we couldn’t even turn on,” Lopez said.

López said those experiences contributed to her belief that Puerto Rico should become independent. She also pointed to the lack of presidential voting rights and voting representation in Congress for Puerto Rico residents as central to her frustration with the island’s current status.

U.S. citizens living in Puerto Rico cannot vote for president, and the island has no senators and only a resident commissioner in the U.S. House of Representatives who cannot vote on final legislation.

“As someone who adores American history, I feel it is only natural that after learning about the great political thinkers of the American Revolution, the people who laid down their lives for life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, those who saw injustice and decided they deserved better, they deserved respect from their leaders. Of course I’d want the same for my people,” Lopez said.

Beyond Puerto Rico’s political status, López said she would like future governments to prioritize education and infrastructure, particularly its public schools and universities.

Jamil Dawahra, 20, of San Juan, Puerto Rico, questioned whether changing Puerto Rico’s political status would address the problem residents currently face.

Dawahra, a second-year studying health policy and administration, said debates over statehood and independence can overshadow issues that occur regardless of the island’s relationship with the U.S.

“Fix the electricity problem, fix the water system, fix the corruption, fix the money laundering, fix the poverty problem, and then we can talk about what’s better for us,” Dawahra said.

Dawahra emphasized that neither independence nor statehood would automatically resolve those problems, arguing Puerto Rico should first address problems within its institutions and infrastructure.

Ana Sofía Torres Candelario, 18, of Mayagüez, Puerto Rico said she would prefer Puerto Rico not move toward independence, but added that dissatisfaction with the current system has more to do with its government than its mere political status.

Torres, a second-year studying psychology and criminology, said she believes problems within Puerto Rico’s government have contributed to discontent with the current system. Corruption, she said, has “completely deteriorated” the island since the hurricane.

“I wouldn’t say for us to change our island to independence, but not maintain it as it is right now,” Torres said. “I would say that a better and renovated government system is actually what we need.”

title: Penn State women’s soccer continues conference play with games against Oregon, No. 13 Washington
author: Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian
description:
After tying in a hard-fought match against Purdue, the Nittany Lions continue with their conference play this week as they travel to Oregon to take on the Ducks this Thursday and the Washington Huskies on Sunday.

Penn State currently sits at 5-2-4 and has been playing like a top team all season. Oregon enters the match at 6-4-2, and No. 13 Washington at 9-1-2, having lost only to Michigan State.

Here’s an outlook on the next week of play.

Oregon

The teams faced off for the first time last season and tied in a 2-2 draw at Jeffrey Field. While the Ducks have home-field advantage this time around, Penn State holds the better record and overall win percentage, making this an important match for the Ducks.

Penn State’s offense has been consistent in each game, with standouts like Aubrey Kulpa scoring her sixth goal of the season to get the tie against Purdue, and Paige Kalal being a key playmaker.

Anna Babcock and Molly Martin have also led the way and will pose tough competition for Oregon’s defense, as the Ducks rely heavily on their back end to make the plays. Goalie Gray Wilson recorded the 100th save of her career in their last game against UCLA and has allowed only seven goals this season.

Oregon defender Miya Alamares will also be important to watch out for, having a track record for being able to predict where attackers are going to shoot, and will be a good challenge for the Penn State offense.

As much as the offense will be crucial to bringing home the win Thursday, Penn State has also seen standout plays from goalkeeper Mackenzie Gress, who has saved .804 percent of the shots taken against her. The wall in front of the net has been protected by defenders like Lily Boyden and Kayleigh Herr, who have started every game, seeing heavy time on the pitch.

Washington

The Nittany Lions will have a harder fight in their game against Washington, as the Huskies have an .833 winning percentage and only one loss.

The last time the two teams met was last season, when the Huskies won 1-0 at Jeffrey Field. The Nittany Lions will look to build on their recent success and take the win, even on the Huskies’ turf.

Washington goalie Tanner Ijams will be hard competition for the Nittany Lion offense, being as strong a netminder as Gress. Ijams often holds her opponents scoreless and is normally in goal for the full 90 minutes.

Huskies’ defenders like Maya Loudd will be difficult to get around and will be a good test to see if Kulpa and Kalal can continue to find each other to make these winning plays, as Kulpa searches for her fifth goal in conference play.

The Huskies come in with a just as stacked team on offense as the Nittany Lions, as top offensive player Jayden Holdenreid holds four goals on the year, and will be an even match for Kalal.

Nicole Crane will also face a test in Huskies’ players Angelica Chou and Maylen Montoya. Crane will have to bring her best to get around the Washington defenders in order to find spots to make open passes, as the two have been solid in Washington’s backline all year.

Penn State will see its toughest match this season Sunday, but also its most evenly matched team. If the Nittany Lions can pull off a win, it’ll be huge for their confidence and could push them into the top-25 in the national rankings and into a top-five spot in the Big Ten standings.

title: Penn State’s most memorable White Out wins
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s White Out game is often the biggest matchup on the schedule each year and has made for some of the most memorable moments in program history.

From the blocked field goal against Ohio State in 2016 to multiple big plays against Michigan throughout the years, the White Out always tends to deliver in some way, shape or form.

Here’s the most memorable White Outs in Penn State history.

2007: First full White Out

The first full-stadium White Out was in Penn State’s victory against Notre Dame in 2007.

Penn State’s defense stifled a Notre Dame offense led by quarterback Jimmy Clausen, and the ground game dominated on the offensive side of the ball.

The Nittany Lions’ first touchdown in front of a full White Out crowd was on Derrick Williams’ 78-yard punt return touchdown, creating one of the loudest moments in Beaver Stadium history.

Running back Austin Scott led the way offensively with 28 carries for 116 yards and two touchdowns as No. 14 Penn State came out on top 31-10 over Notre Dame.

2013: Penn State beats Michigan in 4 OT

One of the biggest wins in White Out history came against Michigan in 2013.

With Bill O’Brien at the helm, Penn State hosted an undefeated Michigan team ranked No. 18 at the time. The Wolverines were led by dynamic quarterback Devin Gardner, but it was Penn State’s offense who stole the show late.

Trailing 34-27 with 35 seconds remaining, Christian Hackenberg threw a ball up and wide receiver Allen Robinson rose above the defenders and came down with it at the 1-yard line. Hackenberg snuck it in from a yard out on the next play to tie the game.

That’s not all the theatrics, however. Michigan kicker Brendan Gibbons missed a 52-yard field goal before the end of regulation and had his 40-yard field goal attempt blocked in the first overtime, a kick that would’ve won the Wolverines the game.

In the third overtime, Gibbons missed a 33-yard game-winning field goal attempt, keeping the score tied at 37. After making his field goal in the fourth overtime, Penn State had the opportunity to win it.

It was all in the hands of running back Bill Belton, who ran for 15 yards on the drive. Belton’s 2-yard rushing touchdown won the matchup and was a program-defining win under O’Brien.

2016: Blocked field goal leads to upset win over Ohio State

Penn State hosted then-No. 2 Ohio State in 2016 in arguably the most memorable White Out ever, and it was a win that changed the trajectory of the program under James Franklin.

The Nittany Lions were heavy underdogs before facing one of the Heisman Trophy favorites in J.T. Barrett. Despite having multiple “Heisman” moments against the Nittany Lions, his efforts came up short.

Penn State trailed 21-7 entering the fourth quarter, and after a 2-yard rushing touchdown from Trace McSorley, the Nittany Lions pulled to within one score.

Ohio State attempted to put the game on ice in the fourth quarter with a field goal attempt that would’ve put the Buckeyes back up by seven. On a career-long attempt, safety Marcus Allen soared above the line and denied the kick, with cornerback Grant Haley scooping it up and ran the length of the field into the end zone, giving the Nittany Lions their first lead of the game.

Penn State’s defense stood strong against Ohio State’s dangerous offense, including back-to-back sacks on third and fourth down to end the game and send Beaver Stadium into a frenzy.

2017: Penn State blows out Michigan

A year after Penn State’s biggest win under Franklin, the Nittany Lions hosted Michigan for the 2017 White Out.

On the second play from scrimmage, Saquon Barkley took it 69 yards to the house and it was all Penn State from there.

Barkley ran for 108 yards and three total touchdowns. The ground game was the main catalyst for Penn State’s blowout win, as McSorley added three touchdowns on 76 rushing yards.

Penn State’s 42-13 win over Michigan marked the second consecutive White Out win, the first time since the first two full-stadium White Outs in 2007 and 2008.

2019: Penn State edges out Michigan in “Mo Bamba” game

Two years later, Penn State once again faced Michigan in the White Out. This time, it was the infamous “Mo Bamba” game, a song that still gets played to this day when the Nittany Lions’ defense is on the field.

After the opening kickoff, Michigan’s offense lost track of the play clock and were forced to call a timeout without even taking a snap from scrimmage after the crowd made it impossible for the Wolverines to hear.

Sean Clifford and wide receiver KJ Hamler combined for two touchdowns, with Hamler totaling 108 receiving yards. Clifford accounted for all four Penn State touchdowns, with three passing and one rushing.

Leading 28-21, Penn State’s defense needed one final stop. On a pass to the end zone, Michigan wide receiver Ronnie Bell was open, but dropped the pass that would’ve tied the game and likely sent it to overtime. Instead, the Nittany Lions held on and defeated Michigan 28-21.

2024: Penn State beats SMU in College Football Playoff

Penn State’s first College Football Playoff game was a White Out.

The Nittany Lions hosted SMU in the first round of the playoffs, and it was a defensive onslaught from the linebackers. Tony Rojas and Dom DeLuca combined for three interceptions, including two pick sixes.

On offense, running backs Kaytron Allen and Nick Singleton combined for three touchdowns and 160 yards on the ground.

In front of the first postseason White Out crown, Penn State took down SMU, 38-10, en route to a College Football Playoff semifinals appearance.

title: Penn State men's hockey notebook | Guy Gadowsky talks team identity, roster rebound
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State opens its regular season with a trip to UConn on Friday night, but before that, the team hosted local media day Tuesday.

After open practice concluded, Guy Gadowsky met with the media in the bowels of Pegula Ice Arena. The 15-year coach hit on a variety of topics, including his team identity.

Here’s all that was discussed in the Nittany Lions first media availability.

Team identity

Gadowsky succinctly described the way he wants his team to play hockey.

“Extremely fast, aggressive. We play to score, and we’re very creative. That’s it in a nutshell,” he said.

This season, Gadowsky doesn’t have a star like Gavin McKenna to play his typical rush attack into, but he has more spread-out talent.

“We might get back to a little more high tempo, everybody deeper, rather than last year, there was two very high octane lines that were used a lot,” Gadowsky said. “I think what you're going to see is scoring by committee.”

That scoring by committee should include Dane Dowiak and Reese Laubach, who were presumed to take on more of the reins this season both on and off the ice.

Captains

In September, the Nittany Lions voted seniors Dowiak and Laubach primary captains.

Dowiak was a captain last year, and Laubach was named an assistant captain midway through the season. Both forwards played large offensive roles on the Frozen Four team two years ago, then they were asked to play entirely different roles last season. Gadowsky said they took it in stride and “didn’t bat an eye.”

“They're incredibly team-first guys,” Gadowsky said. “They are the epitome of the stripes of Penn State hockey. They're tough, energetic warrior guys that score. Yes, we like to score pretty goals off the rush, but we score a lot of hardworking, gritty goals as well and they do both really well. They both have paid their dues and emulate what we want in this program.”

Dowiak went down with a season-ending injury last February and couldn’t contribute to the postseason push, but with 18 points in 27 games, he has the opportunity to make up for the time he missed.

Squashing the injury bug

Dowiak isn’t the only Nittany Lion to miss time last year. Gadowsky’s squad had to play without its primary centers and other key pieces in Keaton Peters and Charlie Cerrato for a significant portion of the year. Peters will take the ice this weekend looking “fantastic,” as the injury appears to be only in the rearview.

They also lost star forward Aiden Fink for much of the year and missed Andrew Kuzma, who played in the Ontario Hockey League, to work his way back from heart surgery after never suiting up for the blue and white during his freshman season in 2024-25.

“The Andrew Kuzma story just warms your heart because he was just a great player that was expecting to play two years ago and was looking so good,” Gadowsky said.

The coaching staff was very excited about Kuzma when he first got to campus, but Penn State Medicine caught a heart issue that caused him to receive surgery. Now, after a year back in junior hockey, Gadowsky called it “wonderful” to see him back in blue and white.

“Even in practice, you can see that he doesn't take one shift for granted,” Gadowsky said. “He's just so grateful to be out here and grateful to have all the resources that he does around here to develop.”

The Nittany Lions will drop the first puck of their 2026-27 campaign in Storrs, Connecticut, on Friday when they take on UConn at 7 p.m. For lines and expected personnel, that insight will all have to wait until the bout with the Huskies takes place.

title: ‘It was time to move on to the Big Ten’ | Justin Poirier brings elite offensive presence to Penn State
author: Dominic Megats I The Daily Collegian
description:
Both nets were pulled halfway to the blue line from the crease in preparation to end the first open practice of the season with a 3-on-2 small-area game.

Both goalies shined for the most part; however, a slap shot from just above the blue line was able to beat freshman netminder Ryder Fetterolf.

The man behind the powerful clapper was one of the top transfers in the offseason for Penn State: Justin Poirier. Quick roars from his group's bench poured onto the Maine transfer as he showed the media in attendance what he brings to the team early.

Poirier used the offseason to jump from the Hockey East to the Big Ten in an effort to play against stronger competition.

“I had a great time at Maine, but it was time to move on to the Big Ten,” Poirier said at local media on Tuesday. “I feel like the Big Ten is maybe closer to the pro level more offensively. If I can use Michigan as an example, (they have) a couple of first-rounders in the NHL. Michael Hage is probably one of the best players in the NCAA. So to play against these guys, it’s going to be a better challenge.”

The sophomore tallied 29 points with 18 goals and 11 assists in 27 games for the Black Bears.

However, before making his way to college, Poirier dominated through three seasons in the QMJHL. Following his second year with the Baie-Comeau Drakkar in which he earned his career-high 82 points, the Salaberry-de-Valleyfield, Quebec, native was drafted in the fifth round of the 2024 NHL Draft by the Carolina Hurricanes.

Taking a leap from conference to conference is no easy decision this early in a collegiate career. Yet, after only one trip to Happy Valley and a meeting with Guy Gadowsky and his staff, Poirier knew he would spend his sophomore year at Pegula Ice Arena.

“I think Penn State is a great fit for me offensively. I came in for a visit and met the coaching staff, and I think it was the perfect fit for me to join Penn State,” Poirier said.

The Quebec product's game has no lack of offense, and his new teammates picked up on that quickly. He possesses a powerful shot and backs it up with elite acceleration.

The Nittany Lions’ forward group lost several key players over the offseason. However, the blue and white added a new group of forwards in hopes of filling the holes they left. Newly assigned captain Resse Laubach understood the importance of Poirier’s addition in particular.

“(Poirier’s) a great player. He’s got a bomb of a shot, so we are excited to have him,” Laubach said. “(I’m) super grateful to have him choose us. He’s definitely going to be a big part of this team for sure. (He) obviously scored a bunch of goals last year, looking to do the same this year — He’s been a great player and great teammate.”

Poirier's offensive ability is sure to land him in the top-six of Gadowsky’s lineup that is primed to continue showing the same “high tempo” they have for the past seasons.

The lines were not made public for the blue and white, but that doesn’t stop the sophomore from developing nerves heading into his first game in for the blue and white.

“I feel like everyone is excited; some of the guys haven’t played for a while, and obviously just the first game of the season; it’s a different emotion,” Poirier said. “Everyone’s been preparing since summer for that game, that moment, and it’s game week. So I feel like everyone is ready.”

title: ‘I absolutely love this place’ | Penn State's Jackson Smith reveals decision to stay, put NHL on hold
author: Chase Fisher | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State defenseman Jackson Smith considered signing his NHL entry-level contract this offseason.

The former No. 14 overall selection in the 2025 NHL Draft revealed he discussed with the Columbus Blue Jackets, the franchise that selected him, his agent and his family about his looming decision.

But Smith, who said in the locker room after last year’s season-ending loss to Minnesota-Duluth in the NCAA tournament, “I’ll remember this feeling, and I’m not going to let it happen again,” ultimately returned to Happy Valley for his sophomore season.

“I could have gone there and tried to make the team, and maybe ended up in the AHL,” Smith said during local media day Tuesday. “But I decided I don't need to rush; I'm still a young kid, I'm trying to play in the NHL for 20 years, not play there when I'm 19, and play there for five years … I want to be the best player I can be when I get there. So if that means taking an extra year in college (I’d do it). I love this place, I was incredibly happy and grateful to be coming back here, and hopefully make the next step.”

Smith, Penn State’s first-ever first-round NHL draft pick, was as advertised his freshman season. The star blue liner finished the 2025-26 campaign with Second Team All-Big Ten honors after ranking second among freshman defensemen in points (26) and leading all Big Ten blue liners in goals (11), which broke a single-season program record.

His seven power-play goals also led the nation among defensemen, while setting the school record for blue liners and jumping to second all-time for all positions.

So imagine what that second-year jump would look like for Smith, who said Tuesday he’s gained 10 to 15 pounds since he came to Penn State in 2025.

“Just my full 200-foot game,” Smith said of what he worked on this offseason. “Just kind of being a bit more of a pest out there, a bit harder to play against in the D-zone, but still not take away from my offensive game — just making a simple play when I need to. Sometimes I feel like I can force some harder plays that don't need to be made at times, but I'm still trying not to take away from the offensive side of my play.”

After losing plenty of upperclassmen leaders this offseason, including Aiden Fink, Charlie Cerrato, Matt DiMarsico and Jarod Crespo, Smith thought it was time to take on more of a leadership role. So he had two conversations with coach Guy Gadowsky — one at the end of last year and one in the summer — to discuss how to maintain the team’s culture.

In his talks with his coach, Smith acknowledged the difficulties of CHL players transitioning to college hockey, as he experienced them himself just a year ago. He decided he wanted to help his new teammates transition to the NCAA quickly.

“I can just bring a lot to the table, especially with the new CHL guys; there's a lot of them coming in now, and there will be more next year,” Smith said. “So it's just teaching them how to play college and teaching them how for the next guys that come in.

Gadowsky spoke on the importance of having a former first-round draft pick, someone of Smith’s stature, take on that role is important, as he’s a player his teammates can lean on.

“It's just a process, and I'm still trying to learn, and I still learn off them, and they learn off me,” Smith said. “It's been fun, but just being a bit more of a veteran, especially with not a lot of our junior class being here anymore, I definitely had to make a step and mature a lot.”

Smith described last season as “the best year of my life,” and said on many accounts that Penn State means so much to him. He said it in the locker room after the Nittany Lions’ season flatlined in Albany, and he echoed that Tuesday in the back corner of Pegula Ice Arena’s media room.

“I absolutely love this place,” Smith said. “Everything about this place — it's just like it's college, like it's just all you have here is college, and it's amazing the atmosphere that we bring to this arena and all the sporting events here. It's pretty incredible. Just being able to walk around with the boys and be so close to everybody. Like, every house is super close; everybody lives really close. So just everything about this place has been incredible. Obviously, the staff here and just everybody in Penn State has been amazing to me and our team — I can't be more grateful.”

title: Penn State still searching for identity as midpoint of season approaches
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Entering the biggest game of the season so far, Matt Campbell and the players made it clear Tuesday that the team is still in search of what defines them, especially on the offensive side of the ball.

“The reality of it is, we lack an identity,” Campbell said. “We lack who we want to be and where we need to be. And I think you know all of those things come back a little bit fundamentally.”

Penn State’s struggles the past two weeks on offense come from the lack of success in both aspects of the unit. With Koby Howard healthy, there was more of an identity, with him being the consistent and reliable receiver.

Now, the team is still searching for answers after five weeks, especially on offense, as it’s found difficulties moving the ball and getting into a rhythm.

“We just don't really know if we’re a run team or a pass team right now, and so I think for all of us, we're going back immediately to the drawing board, going back to the meeting rooms, and figuring out what we could do well,” Rocco Becht said.

With the struggles on offense, Becht is focusing on correcting his accuracy while also working to continue growing the run game. Both issues likely won’t be resolved at the same time, but one getting rectified could help the offense move the ball down the field.

The coaching staff wants to fix things quickly, and going back to the drawing board to find it is part of the process.

“We lack our identity right now across the board, offensively, defensively and on special teams to who we want to be and how we want to win football games,” Campbell said. “I think as we figure out that and continue to unveil that, the ability to be able to lean into a rhythm of a game and how you call the game to kind of lean into winning the football game.”

On the practice field, the players are still putting in the work and practicing to the level the coaches are wanting to see.

Offensive lineman Cooper Cousins has decided to avoid dwelling on the past. His approach to “worry about the next practice” immediately after Tuesday’s practice ended is a mentality that could pave the way to Penn State finding that identity.

Cousins’ mindset is to ultimately help the Nittany Lions’ offense get out of the slump it’s currently in. In the last two games, the offense has scored 26 points combined and has had issues getting into a rhythm.

“We've got great coaches,” Campbell said. “We've got great players. I think the reality is our identity, what allows us to find that consistency that we're lacking to help this offense to continue to move itself forward.”

The toughest part of the schedule is now in front of the Nittany Lions. Penn State hosts USC and has to travel to Michigan and Washington in the next four games, and if the team can’t correct things, the losing streak could last for a while.

It’s a quick turnaround to find all the answers for an offense that put up 291 yards against Northwestern. Despite facing the No. 19 team in the country on Saturday, the Trojans’ defense has struggled, which could be favorable for the spiraling offense.

“Let's make darn sure that the identity that we want to be starts to come out,” Campbell said.

title: ‘Get our swagger back’ | Penn State battles with adversity after 2 straight losses
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Rocco Becht has lost many football games throughout his career. He had back-to-back losses in 2024 and four straight losses in 2025, and now, he’s fallen short in this year’s first two Big Ten games.

But in the past, Becht has bounced back from these losing stretches, winning the remaining games each season. He’s carrying that same mindset right now.

“For me, it's digging back to that 2024 season,” Becht said Tuesday. “What did I do? What did I change to get out of that slump? And I think for me, it was coming to work every single day with a positive attitude.”

Penn State’s next chance to right the ship is the White Out game against No. 19 USC, which is the fourth-highest ranked Big Ten team. On the other hand, the Nittany Lions are coming off a 34-13 loss to Northwestern and are one of the seven teams with an 0-2 record in conference play.

Over the last six quarters of play, the Nittany Lions have struggled in all aspects. The offense has failed to generate significant yardage, specifically on the ground, the defense gave up 413 rushing yards against Northwestern and even kicker Ryan Barker missed a field goal.

While the team isn’t where it wants to be performance-wise, it’s stayed true to its core philosophies and is attempting to grow each week with a positive mindset.

“I went in there with positive vibes throughout the whole facility, and I think that just brings everybody up,” Becht said. “Whatever I’m doing, that’s what the whole team is going to be doing, and so that’s how I carry myself every single day. I’m just going to continue to do what I do and believe what I believe.”

But Becht isn’t the only one who’s faced adversity before. The Nittany Lions lost six straight games last year before ending the year winning five straight. More than 50 of those players are back on this year’s squad and facing similar adversity.

“(I’ve) definitely learned some things about our team last year and about myself individually,” right guard Cooper Cousins said. “I see the capabilities that this squad has. I see how hard everybody works. I see everybody attacking. This team’s hungry to go out there and compete for the best fans.”

Following last week’s loss to Northwestern, several players talked about how the practices were less physical due to the short week. That may not have been the best option, as they then said the game wasn’t as physical as they hoped with several players missing tackles.

This Tuesday, the players said they had one of the most physical practices in a long time, flushing the loss and moving forward.

“No matter what adversity you’re going through, whatever hard times you’re going through, you can’t have a poor me mentality,” Cousins said. “You have to grab your lunch pail and go back to work.”

While the Nittany Lions are facing their first sustained bout of adversity this year, it hasn’t shocked them. They knew before the season this would happen at some point, but they’re now working to fight through it.

“There’s going to be adversity that happens every season, it’s not going to be a Cinderella story,” Cousins said. “I think Rocco has done a really great job and phenomenal job getting us all together.”

With seven more conference games on the horizon, Becht knows the team needs to gain its confidence back from earlier this season because they have the potential to be great.

“I think we just have to get our swagger back and walk around like we're the best person at that position,” Becht said. “We just got to be able to have fun and bring that swagger back.”

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell says his team 'lacks an identity'
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Matt Campbell took the podium at Beaver Stadium on Tuesday after Penn State’s loss to Northwestern. The Nittany Lions are headed into their first White Out game under Campbell at 7:30 p.m. Saturday.

Campbell discussed the team’s lack of a real identity, offensive struggles across the board and gave an update on wide receiver Koby Howard.

Here’s more of what he said.

Team identity

Campbell expressed his frustration regarding the lack of a team identity. He noted Penn State has gone through difficult times in the past and has managed to come back stronger, and while he has confidence in his players and coaching staff, the team “isn’t where it needs to be.”

“The reality of it is, we lack an identity,” Campbell said. “We lack who we want to be and where we need to be.”

He said the team lacks identity on offense, defense and in special teams while not playing to the standard they set for themselves. To improve the culture, he said facing adversity is crucial, something they’re going through right now.

Campbell said the team wasn’t where it needed to be after the Buffalo game, so he’s not surprised by the void in identity at this point because the program is newly growing into it in the first season under his leadership.

“You're trying to mold the culture together, and it's a growth process,” Campbell said. “We have to be better, and it starts with my leadership of making sure we get better. But I have great belief in the humans that we have, and we're just not there right now.”

Rocco Becht, offensive concerns

Rocco Becht has been inconsistent in Big Ten action with just one passing touchdown and three interceptions the past two contests. Campbell noted how when the offense struggles, it can “put a spotlight” on the quarterback’s mistakes.

Although Campbell said Becht needs to be better, he was quick to defend his quarterback and said the entire offensive unit around him needs to be more consistent.

“We need to be better with the other 10 people around him too,” Campbell said. “We need to be better in our pass protection at times, we certainly need to be better in terms of our run game. So we can get him into a rhythm, so he can play with great consistency. We haven't been able to do that, and obviously that is frustrating.”

Campbell noted how the Big Ten is a physical conference, but downplayed the switch from the Big 12. He’s played against Big Ten opponents during his time at Iowa State, and said the physicality of the conference is not the primary concern at this stage.

“Where we're at is trying to build a culture, schemes and foundations, “ Campbell said. “So I think the easy thing to say is, ‘is it a physical problem? Is it a lack of physicality?’ I think some of that shows up when you're so inconsistent in some of the detailed things it takes to play good football.”

Update on Howard

Campbell said Howard is still “a couple weeks away” from his return to the field despite Howard implying he’d be back against Michigan on Oct. 17 via his Instagram story a few weeks ago.

Not having him has added to the difficulties in the passing game, as Campbell said Howard was the player who executed against opponents’ top defenders, a role Chase Sowell is charged with in Howard’s absence.

“One thing that Koby brought was consistency,” Campbell said. “He was the guy that was consistently executing. Koby was the guy that was creating matchups.”

Campbell alluded to how many other players were dealing with offseason surgeries, which could be affecting their play now, and the team needs to have a next-man-up mentality in the wake of injuries such as Howard’s. He said this applies across the board, not limited to the wide receiver room.

“There is a little bit of a process of those guys getting back to where we need them to play with the physicality and the detail we need them to play,” Campbell said. “Those aren't excuses, and that happens in every team in the country. We have to make sure simplicity equals velocity.”

title: Penn State notebook | DC D'Anton Lynn reflects on poor performance from his run defense
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Three days after Penn State’s defense allowed 506 yards to Northwestern, D’Anton Lynn took the podium in Beaver Stadium ahead of the Nittany Lions’ White Out against USC.

Lynn discussed the team’s struggles against the Wildcats on Friday night, the upcoming matchup against his former team and more.

Here’s a look at what he had to say.

Struggles in Evanston

The run game was the most glaring issue in the loss to Northwestern, as Penn State allowed 413 yards on the ground. After watching the film, Lynn said the line of scrimmage was the biggest weakness.

“I don’t know if we won the line of scrimmage once,” Lynn said. “We didn't lose every time, but we didn't win at all.”

As the run defense struggled, Penn State gave up multiple runs of over 30 yards. Several of those came as the result of missed tackles.

Despite those misses, Lynn expressed his confidence in his defense and his linebackers, saying “everyone has done a lot of good things.”

“I would just say the biggest thing is just consistency,” Lynn said. “Consistency in our fits and tackling.”

While the Nittany Lions couldn’t come back and find an answer against the Wildcats, Lynn focused on what it takes to move forward and build success.

“If we have to move guys around, we have to get the different looks,” Lynn said. “We have to put guys in different spots, getting different looks, but put those guys in position to win.”

USC reunion

Lynn spent the 2024-25 seasons at USC before coming to Happy Valley, where he coached against starting quarterback Jayden Maiava during practice.

With the Trojans coming to Beaver Stadium on Saturday, Lynn has experience against Maiava and what he presents offensively. However, coach Lincoln Riley’s playstyle has its difficulties as well.

“He doesn’t have a playbook, he just has plays, and he’s gonna do what his guys do best,” Lynn said. “There's times where he'll present things, and it's like, man, you just don't have an answer for us. You have to keep them guessing.”

The Trojans are coming off a close victory against Washington and are the first top-25 team the Nittany Lions will face this year. Playing against one of the top programs in the Big Ten, Lynn prioritized going back to some of the basics to compete against USC.

“We need to be great on third down,” Lynn said. “We need to be great in the red zone, and we need to stop the run and then don't give them chunk plays.”

Coaching location

Through the first four games of the season, Lynn coached from the booth — a decision that faced a lot of contemplation during fall camp. Against the Wildcats, Lynn started the game in the booth, but moved onto the sidelines after halftime.

“It was just hard to watch from up top,” Lynn said. “Just not being down there with the guys and being able to talk to them, look them in the eye. You don't know what's going on down there, so it just felt better being down there while all that was going on.”

While he made that switch in the second half of Friday’s game, he hasn’t made a decision yet on this weekend’s location, but recognized the benefits of being on the field.

“I just felt better being down there, just making sure, regardless of what the circumstances are, regardless of what's going on on defense, regardless of what's going on on offense,” Lynn said. “When we go out there we have to have the same mentality.”
