title: Weekly Recap | Penn State women’s hockey suffers season opening losses to No. 2 Ohio State
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions opened their season last week with a series against the No. 2 Ohio State Buckeyes at Pegula Ice Arena.

Before the series began, Penn State unveiled both its 2025 AHA Championship and Frozen Four banners in the rafters. The highs of the previous season are followed by this season’s lows, with the blue and white dropping two games to the Buckeyes.

Coach Jeff Kampersal’s squad will look to bounce back against Robert Morris this week in the first series of conference play.

Goalie Competition

The Nittany Lions are currently in a situation that most teams would be pleased to deal with: too much depth.

Both Morgan Stickney and Maddy Campbell performed well against the Buckeyes, a team that has historically had the Nittany Lions’ number. Ohio State entered Happy Valley with an all-time record of 11-2-0 against the Nittany Lions, outscoring Penn State 52-14.

Yet, both goaltenders rewrote the narrative, each allowing two goals in hard-fought matches. Kampersal has made it clear that the pair will be competing for the starting job, and so far both have stepped up to the task.

“Actually, a good problem to have,” Kampersal said after Game 2. “We’ll probably rotate in the beginning to see who kind of emerges.”

The freshman made her debut in the season opener and didn’t disappoint, saving 44 shots to earn a 0.957 save percentage. Thanks to Stickney’s performance, she was awarded AHA Rookie of the Week honors.

While Campbell couldn’t add an accolade to her display, the Courtice, Ontario, native had an impressive showing of her own. Notching 31 saves along with a save percentage of 0.939, the sophomore made her own case as to why she should get the nod.

Despite the intensity of the competition, Campbell has made it clear that there is no bad blood brewing between them.

“We both want to play, and I think that’s really helped us both just be at our top A game,” Campbell said. “I think as we saw this weekend, we both played really, really well… it's a super positive environment for both of us.”

Slow Start Offensively

Penn State’s goaltenders kept both games within reach, but the offense failed to close the gap.

Ohio State held a major advantage in shots on goal throughout both of its wins in Happy Valley, and that is not a recipe for success if you’re the blue and white. The Buckeyes placed 20 more shots on frame than the Nittany Lions in both competitions.

Executing on the power play has also emerged as an issue early, as the Nittany Lions failed to capitalize on any of their opportunities. Penn State simply couldn’t put pressure on the opposing goalie, as six of its nine power plays resulted in fewer than two shots on goal.

“We need more urgency, especially on the power play,” Kampersal said. “It’s not relaxed time; it should be go time.”

Yet, a bright spot has been Grace Outwater’s production so far. The team captain scored in both affairs, and that’s exactly what Kampersal and his squad expect of her.

However, Outwater can’t be the only source of offense for the Nittany Lions. Abby Stonehouse, Nicole Hall, Mikah Keller and company will need to contribute throughout the season for Penn State to live up to its high expectations and with the absence of key forward Matilde Fantin.

MORE HOCKEY COVERAGE

title: Sports Editors Weekly | What's wrong with Penn State men’s soccer after Big Ten losing skid?
author: Myles Hannak & Gianna Dowling | Sports Editors
description:
Editor’s Note: Sports Editors Weekly is a dueling column written by Collegian Sports Editors Gianna Dowling and Myles Hannak. It aims to provide timely debate on Penn State sports performance and news each week.

The Dow has started to crash.

Penn State’s inaugural season with coach Rob Dow started with a bullish outlook after a thrilling comeback over Mercyhurst from 2-0 down to start the year, yet the Nittany Lions haven’t been able to use the debut to fuel a larger run after eight games.

The blue and white only picked up one more win over Yale in a season so far that has seen Dow’s unit stagger to the bottom of the Big Ten with form reaching a real low point during the early campaign.

With the new faces and coach, what is the issue with Penn State after four straight losses to start conference play?

Gianna Dowling: Letting up late

After Monday night's 4-2 loss to UCLA, Penn State has now dropped its last four games and remains winless in Big Ten play.

It’s safe to say that the Nittany Lions are still trying to find their footing in the start of the Dow era, but it's been eight games, so what are the things that’ve been plaguing the blue and white? Well one very big one is letting opponents win, or break away, late in the match.

Sure, an 0-4 conference record doesn’t look good in the standings, but Penn State hasn’t lost by more than two goals in any of these matchups, and two of these games were against ranked opponents.

In the Nittany Lions’ conference opener against Washington, the Huskies scored three goals in the second half en route to a 4-2 victory. A week later, the blue and white faced then-No. 19 Michigan State, falling 1-0 after the Spartans scored in the 84th minute.

Fast forward to last Friday, when Dow’s squad faced another big test against No. 2 Indiana. After going down 1-0 at halftime, Penn State tied the game, but ultimately allowed the Hoosiers to score the game-winning goal in the 76th minute.

Against UCLA, the Nittany Lions fell down 3-0 in the first half, but stormed back in the second to make it a one-goal game. However, a late penalty allowed the Bruins to tag on another goal and seal the deal.

All of these results bring one conclusion: it's been a season full of almosts for Dow’s first year at the helm. Penn State has proven to hang with tough competition, but what the Nittany Lions really need to figure out is how they can play a complete game. Maybe that starts with coaching, or maybe it has to come from the performance on the field.

Myles Hannak: Boom-or-bust playstyle

When Dow came to Penn State, what he did with Vermont gave the Park Avenue Army faith that the blue and white would be back on top. After this season, it looks like the Nittany Lions are destined for a third straight losing season.

Dow’s teams have flash, an attacking approach and a style that feels like it can compete with anyone. Penn State hung in there with some of the nation’s best teams, but also has an approach that can leak simple chances to come back to capitulate the chance at earning points.

The structure and play just don’t look confident in possession; the style feels like it plays for moments and not to sustain a winning style that pressures itself over its opponent. A lot of those moments look to go through forwards Amadou Kone and Etienne Reck, yet when that avenue shuts down, the chances go dry and the opportunities to get a result slim down.

The blue and white may beat some good teams, but it’ll also lose to the games that it’s supposed to win. Expectations weren’t sky-high entering the season with the fresh roster and new era ushering in; slight adjustments need to be made to adapt to the Big Ten and find that consistency.

It may sound like a reason to doubt Dow’s leadership, but that’s not the case; the team showed exactly where it should be in a transitional period like this and perhaps showed more optimism than it needed to. After this season, everyone will have to adapt to a year-long schedule under new rule changes. With a leveled playing field and a longer season, tactical prowess will become what allows Penn State to catch up to its competitors, which Dow should be able to bring given a few tweaks and a cycle to recruit.

title: Penn State held players meeting Monday to ensure team is ‘all on the same page’
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
After Penn State’s first loss of the season against Wisconsin, the players were ready to move on and held a players only meeting on Monday.

“We had a big players’ meeting yesterday, and we all looked at each other and said, ‘We still have everything in front of us. We're going to continue to go out there and grind,’” Rocco Becht said Tuesday.

The meeting was something that came up between Campbell and the veterans on the team because they felt like they needed to have it. It was to ensure the team was “all on the same page” with eight games still to go.

The phrase “being on the same page” isn’t fully what it sounds like according to defensive tackle Keanu Williams.

“It comes into play in the sense of whatever the problems we're having, lay it on the table, and we all kind of got to sit here and you know just talk it out,” Williams said. “Whatever it is we need to talk out, whatever problems we're having, we need to sit there and be on the same page with that.”

Becht was one of the leaders of the meeting, which isn’t surprising considering he’s one of the leaders on the team. His vocal leadership has been highly talked about in the last couple of days, including talking in front of the team following the loss on Saturday.

“Yeah, he played a big role. I think overall, we were just kind of making sure we were all on the same page, kind of going over what we had to do, what our goals for, getting ready for this week,” offensive lineman Trevor Buhr said.

Becht didn’t take much credit for the meeting, despite Buhr mentioning his big role in it. The quarterback was “truly thankful” for Campbell and the other veterans on the team for everything they did and for the closeness of the team.

“Coach Campbell was a big product of why we were able to have those meetings because he's brought us so close together, and he's been able to connect us in a way that I feel like a lot of us haven't been able to do in a while,” Becht said.

The meeting has seemingly already paid dividends in practice, which has ramped up because the coaching staff added a couple more periods to really refine the details.

It’s something that had to be done in a quicker manner given the Nittany Lions play Northwestern on Friday instead of Saturday.

“Detail aspect was a big thing for us this morning,” Buhr said. “That was like the main focus, I'd say, just making sure we're all moving in rhythm. So that was like the big thing this morning.”

The players recognized the game on Saturday wasn’t their best or to their “standard,” and have worked to ensure that kind of play won’t remain the same as the season continues.

While Penn State isn’t ranked in the AP Poll anymore, it has eight more opportunities to prove the type of team it is. It still includes a four-game period when it faces Michigan, USC and Washington, all teams which have been ranked or are currently ranked.

“I think that meeting kind of showed everyone that we're still in this and we believe in one another and we trust in one another, and we know that last Saturday wasn't our best, and that's not us,” Becht said. “And so I definitely expect a different team Friday.”

title: Penn State QB Rocco Becht focusing on ‘everything in front’ after loss to Wisconsin
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
At local media day in early August, Rocco Becht said he was going to have good games and bad games. Throughout his career, he’s made it his priority to “bounce back” from poor performances, and Becht has the opportunity to do just that after being upset by Wisconsin on Saturday.

Becht was off in his Big Ten debut, completing just 41% of his passes for 129 yards and an interception. Although the pick was a tipped ball that fell perfectly into the hands of the Badgers, many of his other throws were tipped, underthrown, too far or behind a receiver.

However, Becht was adamant about moving on to the next game. Becht said Tuesday he and the team “still have everything in front of us.”

“We're going to continue to go out there and grind,” Becht said. “We're still in this and we believe in one another and we trust in one another. I definitely expect a different team Friday.”

Becht noted his connection with wide receiver Brett Eskildsen wasn’t what he wanted it to be, an increasingly important dynamic in the wake of Koby Howard’s injury. Becht pinned the blame on himself for those incompletions.

“We got extra reps today (throwing down the field), and you can never not get enough of those,” Becht said. “That's what our mindset's going to continue to be. Continue to get extra reps so that in the game those things never happen. We just got to be better in those scenarios, and I’ve got to be better.”

While Becht generalized the result, citing “it’s on all of us,” Taylor Mouser shouldered the blame for his quarterback's struggles this weekend.

“I know what Rocco Becht is,” Mouser said. “He's a 10,000-yard passer, and I've known him for three years, and I know how good he is. So when it's not working, I'm gonna always put it on myself because I know how talented he is and the way that he prepares.”

Matt Campbell, however, said there were positives in Becht’s game despite the poor result, saying the main point of concern on Saturday was his consistency. Becht had four completions over 15 yards, and almost found tight end Andrew Rappleyea in the end zone to win the game, but Campbell felt the game was a case of “coulda, woulda, shoulda.”

Going forward, Becht has placed a lot of emphasis on not losing his confidence. Becht has been playing college football for a while, winning plenty of games, but also losing many as well. He wants to use those experiences to carry him through his first loss as a Nittany Lion.

“For me, it’s just continuing to be confident in my game, continuing to go out there and make one play at a time, and not really focus on the past or you know the future,” Becht said. “I’ve got to execute my procedures on each play so we can be better.”

As Penn State prepares to face Northwestern in the first game at the new Ryan Field, Becht said the team is ready to “flush” the loss to Wisconsin and have another opportunity to prove themselves.

“Everyone in this building is excited to go out there and play another football game and to show everyone who we really are,” Becht said. “We didn't really show ourselves last Saturday who we were.”

Penn State wrestling announced its 2026-27 dual schedule, revealing three Bryce Jordan Center duals during the season.

The Nittany Lions open up the season with a previously known matchup against Bloomsburg on Nov. 12 before traveling to Norman, Oklahoma, for the conclusion of a home-and-home against Oklahoma on Nov. 15.

title: Five defendants in alleged cocaine-ring waive formal arraignment hearings, intend to plead not guilty
author: Grace Levy | News Editor
description:
Five defendants in an alleged fraternity-led cocaine-trafficking ring at Penn State have waived their formal arraignment hearings at the Centre County Courthouse, according to court documents.

Agostino Abbatiello, Thomas Robinson, Robert Zanolla, Mohammed Huraibi and Paul Robinson each intend to plead not guilty, according to the documents.

Abbatiello, Thomas and Zanolla all requested jury trials. Huraibi and Paul did not.

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell discusses decision making on infamous 4th-and-1 play
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State picked up its first loss of the season against Wisconsin in Matt Campbell’s first conference game at Penn State.

Campbell met with the media in Beaver Stadium on Tuesday, discussing Wisconsin’s game-winning drive, his decision making and more.

Here’s a look at what Campbell had to say.

Leaving it to chance

Leading 20-17 with less than two minutes on the clock, Wisconsin quarterback Colton Joseph connected with tight end Jacob Harris, who took the ball 72 yards to take the lead. In the days since, there’s been speculation regarding a potential offensive pass interference call against Harris that would’ve negated the touchdown.

“We left it to chance,” Campbell said. “Those great plays, we can make every excuse. Coulda, woulda, shoulda. We put ourselves in a situation where we left it to chance instead of taking care of the situations that we have the ability to take care of and executing what we need to execute.”

Campbell referred to that same mindset regarding plays where Penn State had the ball in great field position but ultimately didn’t score.

The Nittany Lions had three interceptions against Joseph, with the third coming midway through the fourth quarter, presenting an opportunity for Penn State to drain the clock.

Instead, Rocco Becht threw a pair of incompletions and fumbled the snap, resulting in a three-and-out and a punt.

“That’s where the flow of the game, man, you had them, you had the opportunity,” Campbell said. “You go three-and-out and you punt them back the football and you don’t get a first down and you don’t score. Those are gut wrenching.”

Decision making

As Penn State collapsed throughout the fourth quarter, there were several decisions made by Campbell that potentially altered the outcome of the game.

To start the fourth quarter, the Nittany Lions’ offense took the field on a fourth-and-1 with an opportunity to extend the drive, but Campbell ultimately called a timeout and decided not to go for it, punting the ball back to Wisconsin.

“Every decision in this last Saturday's game's gone through your head a million times of, ‘How could you have been better from my standpoint of it?’” Campbell said.

Part of the decision to punt on fourth-and-1 came from knowing Wisconsin’s offense would be operating out of the student section.

“I just felt like that was really the decision-making piece of it, and I really didn't want to screw it up,” Campbell said. “And again, I think you can debate the heck out of it because I have to be honest with you for the last 48 hours.”

Campbell was also asked about the attempts to run the ball on third-and-long, which he said were decisions because “the flow of the game got weird a little bit.”

Getting better opportunities

A major talking point following the game was the lack of production from Penn State’s wide receivers.

With Koby Howard out due to injury, Chase Sowell was the only receiver who caught a pass.

He had six receptions, while the rest of the position group had none.

“Offensively, we just couldn’t find the flow in the game,” Campbell said. “I think part of that was how can we distribute the football better. How can we create more space? I think all those things are real conversations that we continue to have.”

Brett Eskildsen was targeted downfield several times, although each attempt fell unsuccessful.

Campbell said “there were opportunities for guys to make plays,” but that didn’t happen. Part of it came from overthrown and underthrown passes from Becht.

“We have to do a better job of creating those opportunities,” Campbell said. “Then we got to do a better job executing in some of those situations for sure."

title: Penn State notebook | OC Taylor Mouser assesses offense following Saturday's loss
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Offensive coordinator Taylor Mouser met with the media Tuesday following Penn State’s first loss of the season in which the offense totaled a season-low 233 total yards.

Mouser met with the media to discuss his displeasure with how the Nittany Lions spread the ball against Wisconsin and more.

Here’s what Mouser had to say.

Getting tight ends the ball

In Saturday’s game, the only tight end to catch a pass was Benjamin Brahmer, despite the high praise Mouser has given to the room as a whole.

“I still walk out of the game frustrated with my inability to get those guys the ball as much as we should,” Mouser said. “(Andrew Rappleyea)’s one of our best pass catchers and didn't find a way to get him the ball more.”

The tight ends were expected to step up with the absence of wide receiver Koby Howard, who’s out for an extended period of time, but in Saturday’s game, the offense couldn’t get them going. Brahmer only had four catches.

“Especially with Koby out, those three are some of our best pass catchers and we’ve got to find ways to get them the ball in easier ways that we can make those throws,” Mouser said.

Despite the struggles from the tight end room, Mouser still has belief in his position group to get going during a game and help with the rhythm of the offense. Mouser believes the room hasn’t “sniffed” just how good it can be.

Red zone offense

Across the first four games of the season, Penn State has 16 red zone scores, reaching the end zone on 10 of them.

For Mouser, he feels the offense needs to be better in the red zone of scoring touchdowns rather than kicking field goals.

“I'm frustrated with that and it's an ongoing message,” Mouser said. “One of the first things that when Campbell came in on Saturday, like we have to get better at. And for us, it's like establishing our identity, like on the run game, inside the three.”

Penn State had the chance to punch it in from inside the 10-yard line in the first quarter, and failed to do so, having settled for a field goal. When the offense fails to reach the end zone it leads to Mouser and the coaching staff asking many questions.

The offense hasn’t figured out those answers yet, but are working towards getting them to find more success near the end zone.

“We haven't been able to do that, and it's our job as coaches to figure that out,” Mouser said. “But it's certainly a frustrating element of our offense for me and us, something that we have to get better going forward.

Running back rotation

Penn State used all four of its running backs in the first quarter as the unit continues to work through the rotation.

Mouser understands the rotation can take away from any of the four getting into rhythm. While he didn’t commit to saying they’re still going to use a rotation or limiting the running backs used, Mouser said everything is being evaluated.

“Everything after games like that is always being evaluated. Are you playing the right people? Are you putting the right people in a spot to be successful?” Mouser said. “And through the first four games, you hope to have found a rhythm with one of the guys or like a bell cow and you know we haven't yet.”

After the running explosion against Buffalo, the run game was quiet against Wisconsin. But Mouser feels the run game has grown through the first four weeks.

“I think there was a growth standpoint, I feel like an efficiency standpoint in the run game,” Mouser said. “Now we're not seeing the explosive plays in the run game, like I would like us to.”

title: Former Penn State WR Mitchell Tinsley signs with Cincinnati Bengals active roster
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
A former Nittany Lion is headed back to Cincinnati.

Wide receiver Mitchell Tinsley was signed by the Cincinnati Bengals on Tuesday.

Tinsley played in 17 games for the Bengals last season and had eight catches for 116 yards and two touchdowns. Despite reporting to Cincinnati's summer camp this offseason, he signed with the Houston Texans' practice squad, but Tinsley will once again be on the Bengals' active roster.

title: Nittany Lions in the NFL | Parker Washington scores again, Vega Ioane fills in at center
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
While Penn State lost Saturday, several former Nittany Lions had big performances in the NFL.

Wide receiver Parker Washington found the end zone for the second time this season, Juwan Johnson scored over half of the New Orleans Saints’ points and Vega Ioane stepped in as the emergency center for the Baltimore Ravens.

Here’s how the Nittany Lions performed in Week 3.

Juwan Johnson, tight end, New Orleans Saints

Johnson has looked to be one of the best tight ends in the NFL this season, recording 15 receptions and three touchdowns through three games.

Two of those scores came against the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday, where Johnson caught all eight of his targets. His first score came on a short, flat route out of motion, reeling in the 2-yard touchdown.

On his second score, he shed his blocker on the play-action call, running through the end zone for a 1-yard grab.

Johnson finished the day with 53 yards, marking his second straight week catching the ball every time he was targeted and third week with over 50 receiving yards.

It wasn’t all perfect for Johnson, however, who lost a fumble to essentially seal the Raiders’ win.

Vega Ioane, center, Baltimore Ravens

After starting the Ravens’ first three games at guard, Ioane was tasked with playing center late against the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday in Rio De Janeiro, Brazil.

After injuries to the team’s starting center Jovaughn Gwyn and backup center Ethan Pocic, Ioane took the field and helped the Ravens to a last-second, 34-31 victory.

"Obviously, you don't go into a game and hope that that happens, but Vega, man, again — whatever it takes for the team to be successful, I think that was his mindset," Raven’s coach Jesse Minter said.

Mike Gesicki, tight end, Cincinnati Bengals

While former Penn Stater Mike Gesicki didn’t emerge with a win against the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday, he recorded his second touchdown of the season.

Gesicki ran a vertical route from the Steelers’ 26-yard line and flew right past three defenders, finding himself open in the end zone. Gesicki hauled in Joe Burrow’s pass at the 1-yard line as he crossed the goal line for the score.

The nine-year NFL veteran had three catches against Pittsburgh, tallying 37 yards to put him over 100 yards this year.

Parker Washington, wide receiver, Jacksonville Jaguars

For the second time this season, Washington made a highlight-reel touchdown to help the Jacksonville Jaguars earn their second win of the season.

The former Nittany Lion finished with just three receptions for 40 yards, but his 18-yard touchdown helped pad the Jaguars’ 35-6 victory over the New England Patriots.

Washington ran from the slot downfield, diving from the 1-yard line into the end zone to catch Trevor Lawrence’s pass.

Tyler Warren, tight end, Indianapolis Colts

While Tyler Warren didn’t record a touchdown against the Houston Texans, he was crucial in the passing game in the Colts’ 19-17 victory.

Warren tallied nine receptions for 55 yards on Sunday, marking a career-high in catches for the second-year tight end.

The former Penn Stater led the team in receptions, but was second in targets, catching nine of the 10 passes from Daniel Jones.

title: Recruiting roundup | Penn State makes push for in-state 2028 talent with Week 4 visits
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Despite the upset loss to Wisconsin, Penn State had a record number of players visit Happy Valley under Matt Campbell.

Multiple commits returned to campus, while Campbell and his staff set their sights on additional flip targets in the 2027 class. Additionally, the staff continued its push for high-end 2028 talent.

Here’s a look at who headlined the Week 4 visitors to Penn State.

Commits witness Helmet Stripe crowd

Multiple of the current Penn State commits were in town to witness the first Big Ten matchup of the Campbell era.

3-star offensive linemen Ryan Robbins and Jon Sassic both made the trip from the Pittsburgh area for Saturday’s game, while two players from New Jersey also were in attendance.

3-star running back Chukwuma Odoh made his return to Penn State for the first time since his official visit on June 19. 3-star safety Jonathan Galette, meanwhile, was in Happy Valley for the second consecutive week.

In the 2028 class, 4-star quarterback commit James Armstrong visited Penn State for the second time this season after witnessing the home opener against Marshall. Armstrong is ranked as the No. 9 quarterback in the country and No. 5 player in Pennsylvania.

WR flip targets

Along with multiple current Penn State pledges, Campbell is still after some wide receiver targets in the 2027 class.

With only 4-star Landon Blum on board, it appears the Nittany Lions have their sights set on two players who’re committed elsewhere. 3-star Rutgers commit Jamar Taylor visited Penn State for the first time. With Rutgers’ slow start to the season, Penn State could try to add Taylor to its 2027 recruiting class.

Additionally, 3-star West Virginia commit Chase Guers was also in attendance. Guers ranks as the No. 83 receiver in the country and No. 20 player in Pennsylvania in the 2027 class. He received an offer on Sunday following his visit as the coaching staff likely attempts a late push for Guers.

While Penn State has a relatively young receiving core, it’s not a major need in the class, but would be added depth to a receiving room that is still looking to prove itself.

Big 2028 representation

Campbell had some major names in the 2028 class represented on Saturday alongside Armstrong.

The most notable name is 4-star edge rusher George Parkinson IV out of the Philadelphia area. The Malvern Prep product is the No. 88 player in the country, No. 12 edge rusher and No. 2 player in Pennsylvania.

Parkinson has visited Penn State the most of any school, but has offers from other Big Ten programs. Ohio State, LSU, Oregon, Texas A&M, Penn State and Tennessee are in Parkinson’s top six, which he revealed on July 9.

4-star athlete Brandon Murphy Jr. has also been a target to keep in the state. Murphy’s another player that Penn State is in battle with Ohio State for, and could be another player the Nittany Lions target to regain dominance in the state. He’s the No. 4 player in Pennsylvania.

4-star wide receiver AJ Lopez Jr. made the visit from New Jersey, joining his high school teammate Odoh, who’s committed in the 2026 class. The No. 11 player in New Jersey doesn’t have as many offers as other players in the class who were at Beaver Stadium on Saturday, with the most notable coming from UCLA, Virginia Tech and Nebraska.

The push to control the New Jersey area was notable with other visits. Tight end Quinn Weber, safety Mekhi McNair, wide receiver Dontaye Day-Thompson and defensive lineman Jayden Beckley were all at Beaver Stadium The 3-star recruits all rank inside the top 20 in the state in the 2028 class.

Penn State has more commits in the 2027 class from New Jersey than any other state, proving it to be a clear pipeline state for the new state.

With the biggest recruiting visit group under Campbell in attendance, it’s the last time players will be able to visit before what’s consistently the biggest recruiting weekend of the season — the White Out.

title: Off the Record | My oh my, drunk alumni
author: Miss Behave I The Daily Collegian
description:
Editor’s Note: Off the record is a weekly column written by a fourth-year Collegian staffer writing under an alias. It aims to promote a space for honest conversations about love, sex and relationships. Those interested in sharing their experiences or submitting a topic are invited to do so through this anonymous form.

Although Penn State’s drinking culture is relatively heavy year-round, football season attracts an even bigger crowd with more alumni — which means even more beer. It’s important for students and graduates alike to practice responsible drinking in order to look out for themselves and each other.

Penn State alumni put their blue and white back on and relive their Nittany Lion days cheering in the stands of Beaver Stadium, but when there’s football, there’s tailgating. The combination of all the latter can lead to inevitable undignified behavior.

It’s not uncommon for current students to feel uncomfortable with drunk alumni tripping, falling and publicly urinating (gross, I know) when they're in town for a game. Mutual respect is crucial in ensuring all parties are having a good time.

Of course, alumni should have fun at their alma mater. However, sometimes they cross a line.

Immaturity toward college students shouldn’t be tolerated. I don’t care if “the alcohol has that effect” or “they’re just drunk.”

All Nittany Lions, current or former, should know how to handle alcohol responsibly. We shouldn’t reach a point of intoxication that allows us to forget how to act appropriately.

Older men asking to take pictures with college women they don’t know is never OK. Older adults screaming at college students is never OK, just as when the roles are reversed. Of course, I’m aware these older adults are likely not reading this. While I cannot tell them directly to grow up, I can tell you how to deal with the uncomfortable encounters.

Safe drinking

We can’t criticize others if we don’t practice safe drinking ourselves.

If you choose to drink, always make sure to do it with people you trust. If you’re caught in an uncomfortable situation, you’re better off being surrounded by true friends who would help you rather than those who are unsure about whether or not they should intervene. While we should all be responsible for ourselves, looking out for each other is just as important.

A large part of drinking safely is knowing your limits. As students, it’s important to know when to stop, and it’s no different for alumni. Older adults believe they can handle the same amount of alcohol their 21-year-old self could, and I shouldn’t even have to say it, but they can’t. Eat, drink water and don’t push yourself. You don’t need another shot.

Don’t accept random drinks

Whether it’s at the bars or outside the stadium in the tailgate lots, a drink offer is always possible.

A good rule of thumb is to never accept a drink from anyone you don’t know. While a free drink may sound enticing in the moment, spiking drinks or using them as an excuse to stay near you is not a challenge. It’s better to be safe than sorry.

We would like to believe that people don’t have ill intent, but it’s so important to always play defense — especially for a college woman.

A side note I would like to add is that if you’re at the Lion’s Den and an older man is there, immediately walk the other way. While alumni at the bars is totally normal, that doesn’t include the Den. Alumni at an underage bar is a huge red flag. If they peaked at the Den and just want to relive their glory days, that’s a whole other issue they should sort out.

Don’t engage

At the end of the day, I find it’s best to ignore reckless behavior altogether.

You never know how a drunk person could react to a situation, so avoid starting fights. If you can avoid eye contact, you should. While it’s important to stand up for yourself, not engaging is the best bet when a drunk person is involved.

If it’s physical, though, kick him where the sun don’t shine.

Until next time,

Miss Behave

title: Penn State men’s hockey to face early nonconference challenges
author: Dominic Megats I The Daily Collegian
description:
No. 17 Penn State will play eight nonconference teams in the 2026-27 season, including its first-ever Ice Breaker Tournament in Connecticut.

The Nittany Lions are set to travel for five games, one being a neutral-site game in New Jersey against Army at the Prudential Center.

With questions surrounding a team that lost several key players in the offseason, a nonconference stretch that consists of two early ranked opponents will give Guy Gadowsky an idea of what his team will look like heading into conference play.

Here’s how the slate shapes up outside the Big Ten for the blue and white.

No. 15 UConn

The season opens away from Pegula Ice Arena and inside the Toscano Family Ice Forum, home of No. 15 UConn.

It was a historic game for the blue and white the last time it faced off against the Huskies. Matt DiMarsico scored the game-winning overtime goal against UConn in the 2025 NCAA quarterfinals, sending the Nittany Lions to its first Frozen Four in program history.

The Huskies finished last season with a 20-13-5 record, losing the Hockey East Championship game to Merrimack College and to Michigan State in the NCAA Regional. Ryan Tattle led his team with 32 points last season. However, with the senior graduating, UConn will look towards Joey Muldowney to fill the role after leading the Huskies in goals with 17.

Sacred Heart

The second game in the Ice Breaker Tournament for the Nittany Lions will be Sacred Heart. The blue and white hold a 6-0 record over the Pioneers, with the last meeting between the squads in the 2019-20 season.

Sacred Heart finished second in the AHA with a 23-14-3 record. The Pioneers ended their season with a loss to Bentley in the conference championship game.

Felix Trudeau led his team in goals with 25 and points with 48. However, he departed along with three other seniors who were close behind him in points. The closest returning Pioneer is Gavin Bryant who finished with 21 points, entering his sophomore season.

No. 7 Quinnipiac

Penn State then turns to another ranked opponent in No. 7 Quinnipiac. This game also marks the Nittany Lions’ home opener. The two teams have only played each other once, dating back to the 2024-25 season in which the Bobcats won 3-2.

Quinnipiac finished its recent season 27-10-3, losing to Clarkson in the ECAC quarterfinals. The Bobcats made it to the quarterfinals of the NCAA tournament, ultimately falling to then-No. 2 North Dakota.

Ethan Wyttenbach had a remarkable first year with Quinnipiac, leading the country in points with 59. Due to this performance, Wyttenbach was named the National Rookie of the Year.

Robert Morris

The Colonials roll into town for one game in Happy Valley, with the second game away later in the season. Penn State holds an 8-4 record over Robert Morris after winning the last matchup 6-2 in 2020.

Robert Morris finished 16-21-3 overall and third in the conference. Although having a subpar season, the Colonials earned a spot in the conference semifinals. Sacred Heart won the best-of-three in its finale with a score of 5-0.

Before transferring to Maine this offseason, Tanner Klimpke led the Colonials in points with 31. The Calgary, Alberta, native departed from the team, leaving Jackson Reineke as one of the more successful returning players. The senior finished with 26 points in his recent campaign.

Canisius

The final nonconference series before Penn State begins Big Ten play comes against Canisius. The Nittany Lions hold a dominant 8-1 all-time record over the Golden Griffins.

Canisius finished 17-16-2 last season, losing in the first round of the AHA playoffs. However, the team will have a couple of returners fresh off successful seasons.

With point-leader Grant Porter graduating, returners Walter Zacher and Rhys Chiddenton will look to build off a solid junior season heading into their final year with the Golden Griffins.

Princeton

Gadowsky will face his old team again as Princeton is set to visit Happy Valley in November. The Nittany Lions head coach is tied with his former team at 1-1-1.

The Tigers finished their most recent season with a successful 18-13-3 record, landing them fourth in the ECAC. Princeton stormed through the conference playoffs, reaching the championship. An undefeated run ultimately was defeated at the hands of Dartmouth in the ECAC championship game.

Princeton welcomes back Kai Daniells for his senior year. The Whistler, British Columbia, native led the team with 39 points and 19 goals. Also returning is Jake Manfre for his third season. Manfre finished behind Daniells with 15 goals.

Army

Penn State will take on Army for its first series in December. The Nittany Lions will head to New Jersey with the first game of the series held inside the Prudential Center, before returning home for Game 2.

Army is coming off a forgettable season after going 12-17-6 and losing in the first round of the AHA tournament.

However, several key forwards from last season are returning. Jack Ivey led the squad with 28 points and 14 goals. Behind him are Nils Forselius with 26 and Ben Ivey with 24.

Niagara

The Nittany Lions will ring in the new year with their final nonconference series against Niagara. Penn State will spend New Year’s Eve at home for Game 1, then travel to New York for Game 2.

Similar to Army, the Purple Eagles are coming off an unsuccessful year, going 13-23-1. However, Niagara was able to knock off Army in the first round of the AHA tournament before losing to Sacred Heart in the quarterfinals.

The Purple Eagles will be without point-leader Declan McDonnell heading into the season. Behind him were Jacob Malliet and Maxim Muranov with 22 points and eight goals, respectively. Both players are set to return for Niagara.

title: Penn State men’s soccer doomed by penalties in 4-2 loss to UCLA
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State welcomed UCLA to Jeffrey Field on Monday night, seeking its first conference win. The Nittany Lions hadn’t won since Sept. 4 against Yale, and that trend continued against the Bruins with a 4-2 loss.

Rob Dow’s squad is in the midst of a tough four-game stretch. After losing to No. 19 Michigan State at home, the team traveled to Bloomington and lost a hotly contested match 2-1 to No. 2 Indiana. UCLA is the defending Big Ten champion, and then on Friday, No. 3 Ohio State comes to town for the White Out.

1st Half

Penn State flew out of the gates, putting pressure on the UCLA back line in the opening stages of the contest. In just the second minute of the game, senior Morgan Marshall ripped a shot at the lower right corner of the net, but Ryan Tiltack went full extension to make the save.

UCLA quickly turned it right around and got on the board in the sixth minute.

The Bruins took a shot from just left of the box, and Daniel Peluffo-Wiese parried it right to UCLA’s Philip Naef, who buried it for his first goal of the season.

The Nittany Lions tried to bounce back twice in the next few minutes, but were tripped up by offensive fouls each time. First, it was Marshall taking down a Bruin behind the play, then Etienne Reck thwarted his own chance by hooking Victor Ciaurriz right in front of the net. The senior forward got a step on Ciaurriz, but he left his elbow behind and was whistled for the foul.

Another Penn State chance turned into a counterattack by UCLA forward Finot Pie. The Barcelona, Spain, native was alone with Peluffo-Wiese, but he fired just left of the net.

Peluffo-Wiese then picked up two more saves as UCLA continued its relentless attack.

The match began to get chippy in the 17th minute when a scuffle broke out between Penn State’s Toby Grant and UCLA’s Henry Jeffcott. The original foul was on Jeffcott, but both players received yellow cards for their roles in the scuffle.

The Nittany Lions saw a perfect chance to equalize pass right before their eyes when Reck and Ciaurriz had their second run-in of the evening. Grant played the ball ahead to Reck in front of the net, but Reck was tied up with Ciaurriz, and he was called for a foul. The Park Avenue Army and the Penn State bench begged for a penalty kick, but none was awarded, even after a Dow challenge.

After three Penn State substitutions, the Bruins cashed in on their consistent possession with nine minutes remaining in the first half. Junior midfielder Jaime Amaro carried it into the box, where he slid it to Logan Hall, who tapped it over to Diego Castano with a great look at the net. The fifth-year forward slipped his shot right under Peluffo-Wiese, extending the lead to 2-0.

It didn’t take long for the Bruins to strike again. A scoring chance for Penn State turned into a UCLA counterattack, and sophomore Moritz Weber committed a foul just inside the box, giving the Bruins a penalty kick.

Peluffo-Wiese guessed the right direction, but UCLA’s Shakir Nixon slid it right underneath his gloves to take a 3-0 lead in the final stages of the half.

As the half came to a close, Dow’s squad made the walk into the new soccer complex looking sour.

2nd Half

UCLA picked up right where it left off after halftime. Chances came early and often for the Bruins, but the Penn State back line held strong.

In the 67th minute, the Nittany Lions brought Reck back into the game for an offensive spark, and he certainly did his job.

Just three minutes after his reentry, Reck, a Marl, Germany, native took a through ball from freshman Peter Doran between four defenders, finally putting Penn State on the board.

Now down 3-1, Reck didn’t stop there. In the 78th minute, the junior skirted past the outstretched body of Tiltack and scored unassisted to cut the deficit to 3-2.

Three yellow cards and several thwarted Penn State chances later, UCLA put the final nail in the coffin. Peluffo-Wiese came flying out of his net and took down UCLA’s Oliver Roche in the box, giving the Bruins their second penalty opportunity of the game.

With just 29 seconds remaining, Nixon extended the lead to 4-2 from the penalty spot and iced the match.

Peluffo-Wiese was strong in goal nearly the entire game, but fatal mistakes in the box and the sheer number of UCLA opportunities sank the Nittany Lions.

Up Next

The Nittany Lions are back at home Friday to take on No. 3 Ohio State in the White Out.

title: Penn State field hockey ends 3 game losing streak, defeats Bucknell on the road
author: Owen Lomotan I The Daily Collegian
description:
Following its three straight losses to Princeton, Maryland, and Monmouth in its last three games, the pressure was on for Penn State field hockey to bounce back on the road against Bucknell.

The blue and white traveled to Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, to attempt to get back in the win column against a team that had never beaten them in the history of the matchup between the two teams. That continued with a 3- 0 win for the program.

Within the first few minutes of the opening quarter, Penn State traded blows with the Bison, the ball moving back and forth across the field.

With 11:12 to go in the first quarter, junior forward Ella Gaitan put in the first points for the Nittany Lions, giving Penn State an early 1-0 lead over Bucknell.

Just seconds later, Gaitan’s next shot went just wide of the net, nearly extending the lead to two for the Nittany Lions.

The first penalty corner for the blue and white came with 7:16 remaining in the first period. Sophomore forward Joji Purdy’s shot was blocked by the Bison defense, keeping the lead at one goal.

The second penalty corner for Penn State came with 4:37 remaining. Gaitan’s shot bounced off the left post and missed, keeping the lead 1-0 for the Nittany Lions.

The opening quarter ended with the blue and white leading by one score over the Bison.

The opening minutes of the second quarter went similarly to the first, with both teams playing a tight-knit style of play at a fast pace on both ends of the field.

Junior forward Natalie Freeman’s shot with just above 9 minutes remaining in the second went just wide, leaving the lead untouched.

Freeman’s shot just over two minutes later hit the back of the net, extending the Nittany Lion lead to 2-0 with 7:21 remaining in the first half.

The final minutes of the second quarter were full of physical defensive play highlighted by the Bison’s ability to stop the Penn State attack in the shooting circle several times over.

The Nittany Lions entered halftime with a 2-0 lead over Bucknell.

The third period began with Penn State putting solid pressure on the Bison defense in the shooting circle.

With 11:34 remaining, junior goalkeeper Aby Deverka made her first crucial save to keep the Nittany Lion lead intact.

The third penalty corner for the blue and white came with 11:01 remaining. Gaitan's shot was saved by the Bucknell defense and Purdy’s shot soon after was also stopped.

Penn State’s fourth penalty corner of the game came with 7:10 remaining. The Nittany Lions fumbled the shot opportunity and they weren’t able to score a third goal.

Bucknell’s first penalty corner came with 5:16 remaining. The Nittany Lions defense held firm after the Bison also failed to get a shot off and bring the deficit to just one goal.

The Nittany Lions earned their fifth penalty corner with just under three minutes remaining. Purdy’s two quick shots both came up short, leaving the lead at two goals.

Penn State’s sixth penalty corner came with 1:25 remaining. Gaitan’s shot missed wide, forcing a seventh penalty corner. Gaitan’s next shot was stopped by Bison senior goalkeeper Sarah Althouse with just under a minute remaining.

The blue and white earned their eighth penalty corner with 13:19 remaining in the fourth quarter. Gaitan’s shot was again blocked by Althouse, forcing a ninth penalty corner.

Sophomore midfielder Laura Pyle’s shot went high over the net and it was blocked again by the Bison defensive line, keeping the lead at two.

Freeman’s shot with just under 11 minutes remaining was deflected away and the Nittany Lions couldn’t stop their cold streak.

Bucknell’s second penalty corner came with 9:20 remaining. The Bison shot was blocked and another chance was awarded to the orange.

The blue and white defense held firm, and the score remained the same.

The Nittany Lions earned their tenth penalty corner with 8:18 remaining in the game. The Bison defense held, but Penn State got another chance.

Purdy’s shot failed to cross the goal line, and another corner was awarded.

A new season-high thirteenth penalty corner was awarded, but freshman defensive back Lily Holmes failed to convert her opportunity.

Bucknell’s third penalty corner with 7:30 remaining was stopped by graduate midfielder Camryn Standish, who deflected the Bison shot wide.

Gaitan’s close-range shot gave the Nittany Lions a three-goal lead over the Bison with 3:45 remaining in regulation.

Penn State’s fifteenth penalty corner came with 1:57 remaining. The Nittany Lions failed to convert and another chance was given.

The blue and white couldn’t convert once again and the score remained 3-0.

The Bison earned their fourth penalty corner with 21 seconds remaining in regulation. The Nittany Lion defense was able to hold off the Bison attack to keep the score 3-0.

The Nittany Lions were able to earn their first road win of the season, defeating Bucknell 3-0 in regulation.

Up next

The Nittany Lions will face Rutgers on Friday at 3 p.m. in New Jersey.

title: Watercolor art, farmer’s market | Here’s what’s happening in the valley
author: Alli Satterfield | The Daily Collegian
description:
As the Penn State football team travels to an away game this weekend, you may be asking yourself what to do in State College. There’s still a lot to do in the valley to keep you busy, while you cheer on the Nittany Lions from afar.

Here’s what’s happening in the valley this week.

Monday, September 28

Never Stop Learning - Adult Literacy Open House

This free event, hosted by the State College Area School District, Schlow Centre Region Library and Midstate Literacy Council, is an open house intended to teach attendees about free community resources and services like Wifi, computer help, career support, ESL instruction and library cards.

The event will be held from 6 to 7:30 p.m. at the Schlow Library, and new adult readers and English language learners are encouraged to attend.

Penn State Men’s Soccer vs. UCLA

Sick of back-to-back home American football games? The Penn State men’s soccer team will take on UCLA at Jeffrey Field, which may provide you with a much needed change of scenery after Penn State’s performance in the Wisconsin game.

The game will start at 7 p.m. on Monday, and it’s free to attend.

Wednesday, Sept. 30

Yoga and Mindfulness at the Palmer

A collaboration between the Palmer Museum of Art and Penn State Health Promotion and Wellness, this free event offers mindfulness, meditation and yoga, as well as an opportunity to drop into the Palmer. People at every experience level are encouraged to attend. The event, held from 12:30 to 1:30 p.m., is the perfect opportunity to leave all your beginning of semester stress in September and enter October with a fresh mind.

Thursday, Oct. 1

Spooky Plants Walk

In honor of the first day of October, Thursday, the Arboretum is hosting its “spooky plants walk” at 4 p.m. The walk begins at the Overlook Pavilion at the Arboretum, and it includes storytelling about witches, werewolves and all things scary.

Register for the free event ahead of time on the arboretum’s website.

Gallery Conversation | America Works: Building and Sustaining the Nation

Want to start out October by learning something new (or in this case – old)?

This free event, which begins at 6 p.m. at the Palmer Museum of Art, invites attendees to explore a special exhibition, “America Works,” alongside a conversation between faculty curators and Penn State’s School of Labor and Employment Relations professors Kate Ragon, Carla Lima Aranzaes and Arthur Matthews.

Good Times Line Dancing - Country Night @ Happy Valley Live

Sticking with the theme of learning something new, from 6 to 9 p.m., Happy Valley Live will have free line dancing open to all ages. The event is open to all skill levels, so it’s the perfect opportunity to stomp out your end of the week stress.

Happy Valley Live will have an instructor to lead dances in beginning, intermediate and advanced skill sets.

Friday, Oct. 2

Downtown State College Farmer’s Market

The Downtown State College Farmer’s Market is back for the 2026 season. Stop by Locust Lane from 11:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. on Friday to pick up your favorite vegetables, baked goods and local finds all produced in Centre County.

Watercolor Materials Lab

If you’re looking to get in touch with your artistic side, this free lab at the Palmer Museum of Art is a hands-on watercolor experience is the perfect chance.

Located in the Mimi Barash Coppersmith Studio Classroom, the Palmer Museum of Art invites you to join Penn State art history professor Sarah K. Rich and the staff of the Center for Virtual and Material Studies (CV/MS) to explore historic watercolor paints in an experience complementing the exhibition “Out of the Shadows: Drawing and Watercolors by American Women."

Space is limited, so registration via Microsoft Form, is required for this event. Participants will receive a confirmation email after registering.

Jazztrax at the Winery

Mount Nittany Vineyard and Winery is hosting a jazz night, with Jazztrax performing, on Friday from 5 to 7 p.m. There is no cover for this event, and seating is first come, first serve.

The vineyard encourages people to bring their own picnic supplies and food, but there will also be charcuterie items available for sale.

Splintered Sunlight

What better way to spend a Friday night in October than with the dead? Splintered Sunlight is bringing their Grateful Dead tribute to the Friedman Auditorium at the State Theatre on Friday. The show is at 8 p.m., and tickets are available for sale on the State Theatre website.

Saturday, Oct. 3

Fall Fest

‘Tis the season for fallen leaves, pumpkin spice and plenty of festivals. The Downtown State College Improvement District will be hosting their Fall Fest from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. on Saturday. The free event will have pony rides, face paint, food vendors and more.

26th Annual Wasson Farm Fall Fest

title: Big Ten roundup | Conference play kicks off, Michigan, USC fall
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
A majority of Big Ten programs kicked off their conference schedule this weekend, delivering several big performances and upsets.

Wisconsin had a second-half comeback against Penn State, Oregon upset USC in Los Angeles and Michigan experienced déjà vu from its last-second victory against Western Michigan in Week 1, although this time in favor of Iowa.

Here’s how the Big Ten fared in Week 4.

Dylan Raiola leads Oregon

Trailing 7-3 to USC, Dante Moore and Oregon were marching down the field in what finished as a touchdown-scoring drive. However, linebacker Desman Stephens II ended both his and Moore’s evenings with a targeting penalty.

Moore was ultimately carted off the field and taken to the hospital, where he was diagnosed with a concussion, while Stephens was ejected. Former Nebraska starting quarterback Dylan Raiola came on in relief and delivered a masterclass performance to upset the Trojans.

Raiola’s first drive resulted in a 3-yard touchdown pass, giving Oregon a lead it held the rest of the game. He finished with 289 yards and a pair of touchdowns.

The Ducks had a pair of 100-yard receivers in tight end Jamari Johnson and running back Dierre Hill Jr. despite neither finding the end zone. Johnson and Hill tallied 119 and 105 yards, respectively, including a 62-yard catch from Hill.

On the other side of the ball, Jayden Maiava recorded 326 yards and two touchdowns for USC.

Big Ten nail-biters

Kicking off at 11:05 p.m. ET, Minnesota and Washington’s matchup came down to the final play of the game as the Golden Gophers earned their first Big Ten win of the year.

The Huskies capitalized off an interception against Minnesota quarterback Drake Lindsay, taking the ball down the field for a touchdown to make it a one-score game in the fourth quarter. After a field goal from Minnesota, Washington quarterback Demond Williams Jr. led his squad for another touchdown with less than two minutes on the clock.

Washington held Minnesota to a three and out, but couldn’t progress down the field for the game-winning drive, ultimately falling 27-24.

Coming off a national championship last year, Indiana had its first true test of the season against Northwestern on Friday night.

Northwestern put together a solid drive in the third quarter to make it a five-point game before Indiana made it a two-score game, 29-20, with less than two minutes to play. Kicker Jackson Kleather put a last-minute field goal on the board for the Wildcats, although it was too little too late, losing 29-23.

Shocking finish in the Big House

Michigan earned its first loss of the season as Iowa’s last-second touchdown attempt was successful.

As time expired, Iowa quarterback Hank Brown found wide receiver Reece Vander Zee in the front corner of the end zone, dragging his toes for the game-winning score.

The Wolverines had the better offensive performance between the two teams, recording 429 yards compared to Iowa’s 285 yards. Quarterback Bryce Underwood had a much better showing than the first few games this season, throwing 276 yards for two touchdowns and an interception.

Brown was a major catalyst in the team’s victory with 227 yards and two touchdowns. However, it was running back Braeden Jackson who returned a kickoff 99 yards for a touchdown to kickstart the Hawkeye’s scoring.

Conference blowouts

The Bob Chesney era at UCLA continued its hot start, as the Bruins dominated Maryland 54-3.

Both aspects of the offense saw strong performances. Quarterback Nico Iamaleava threw for 209 yards and a touchdown, while the run game produced 266 yards and four touchdowns.

However, it was the defense that was the primary driver against Mike Locksley’s squad. The Bruins recorded four interceptions, including two pick sixes, on Maryland’s Malik Washington. They allowed just 181 yards of offense, sacking Washington twice and tallying seven tackles for loss.

Ohio State also beat Illinois by a large margin, winning 42-19 at home.

The Julian Sayin and Jeremiah Smith connection was unstoppable, as Smith finished the day with 217 receiving yards and four touchdowns. Sayin threw 27-for-36 with 367 yards, while the run game tacked on another 151 yards on the ground.

The Fighting Illini didn’t struggle to move the ball offensively with 462 total yards. However, the team stalled out many times, settling for a pair of field goals and two failed fourth down conversions.

title: Stock up, stock down | Penn State’s offense stalls, interceptions rise in first loss of the season
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Matt Campbell had his first loss at Penn State in a 24-20 upset to Wisconsin in the Homecoming game on Saturday.

The Nittany Lions were generally inconsistent throughout the game, especially on offense. The defense was mostly strong until the Badgers’ final two drives of the game.

Here’s what improved and regressed in Penn State’s conference-opening loss.

Stock down: Rocco Becht

Rocco Becht put in his worst performance as a Nittany Lion so far when Penn State needed him most. For the first time this season, Becht didn’t have a touchdown through the air, as he went 12-for-29 with 129 passing yards and an interception.

Becht only connected with Chase Sowell and Benjamin Brahmer. He wasn’t able to get Andrew Rappleyea, Gabe Burkle, Zay Robinson or Brett Eskildsen going.

Sowell had the better performance, making six receptions for 70 yards, but only one receiver getting the ball doesn't bode well for Penn State’s passing game going forward.

Eskildsen was slated to have a big game with Howard out. However, Becht either overthrew him or didn’t put enough on the ball, leading to his fastest receiver having to slow down and lose key separation.

The tight end room was silent aside from Brahmer’s three catches in the first quarter. Brahmer finished the game with four catches on eight targets for a mere 36 yards.

“I got to be better for the offense,” Becht said postgame. “I got to be better for this team. I can't put us in, you know, scenarios where our backs are backed up and we got to have a big play.”

Stock up: Forcing turnovers

After recording two interceptions in the first three weeks, the Nittany Lions had three on Saturday and gave the offense every chance to take a bigger lead.

Cornerbacks Josiah Zayas and Daryus Dixson had interceptions on back-to-back drives in the second quarter, both resulting in scores. Zayas’ was the first pick six of the season, while Dixson’s interception set up Becht’s rushing touchdown.

Linebacker Tony Rojas grabbed the third interception of the game, and his second of the season, in the fourth quarter.

“It's nothing new,” linebacker Kooper Ebel said. “We see that every week, every day at practice. It's a tribute to how they show up and work every day.”

Stock down: Coaching

Throughout the game, Penn State’s offensive woes and disciplinary issues landed it in third-and-long situations deep in its own territory. Here, Mouser oddly called for runs.

Although the running backs were able to gain seven or eight yards on some of these carries, Penn State still had to punt.

Additionally, late in the first half, Penn State had over a minute on the clock to drive down the field from its own 33-yard line. Campbell decided to burn the clock, giving up on potential points before Wisconsin started the third quarter with possession.

“I felt like we were playing such good defense there that I just didn't want to put the team at risk,” Campbell said. “But I think that'll eat at me.”

At the start of the fourth quarter, Penn State had a crucial decision to make on a fourth-and-1 on its own 38-yard line. Nathan Tiyce came out to punt the ball when the team had the opportunity to go for broke and have another set of downs to make things happen.

“I wish we could have went for that fourth-and-1 for sure,” running back James Peoples said. “But there were multiple times in that game where I feel like we could have took the momentum back.”

Stock up: James Peoples

Peoples was the fourth running back to appear, and he immediately made an impact as Penn State’s most efficient rusher.

While he finished the game with 67 rushing yards — averaging only 4.8 yards per carry — he had the most explosive gains and a long of nine yards. Peoples utilized his agility rushing between the tackles, and if the playcalling allowed him to rush on more manageable second down situations, the ground game would’ve seen more success.

“We knew that was gonna be a four quarter game, so we needed to battle,” Peoples said. “I just need those details on my part first. I'm attacking the building and the intent that we need to be better with.”

So far, Carson Hansen has been the starting running back, but that’s changing as the season goes on. Peoples and Quinton Martin Jr. have put in better performances as of late, with Peoples out-carrying them by far in the Big Ten opener.

Stock down: Quinton Martin Jr. and Carson Hansen

When the passing game wasn’t clicking, the coaching staff trended toward the running backs, a room that’s had the most struggles this season. The running backs only averaged 3.3 yards per carry against Wisconsin.

Martin had a big game against Buffalo in Week 3 with 100 rushing yards after not playing against Temple the week prior. However, he wasn’t utilized in the same way against Wisconsin, ending the game with 14 yards on six carries.

Hansen equally struggled to establish himself, with only four carries on the day, three of which were in the first quarter, and rushed for 11 yards.

It appears as though Hansen has slipped far in the depth chart so far this season. He had shaky results against nonconference opponents, and when it came time to work against a Big Ten defense, the coaching staff was quick to take him off the field.

title: Week 4 report card | Offense struggles, defense collapses late in Penn State’s loss to Wisconsin
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State began its Big Ten slate with a loss to Wisconsin, which upset the Nittany Lions with two straight touchdowns in the fourth quarter.

Despite controlling a majority of the game, Penn State couldn’t close it out late, with many areas of its game struggling throughout the entirety before the late collapse from the defense.

Here’s how I’d grade Penn State’s offensive and defensive units after the loss.

Overall grade: D

Coaching staff: C-

Matt Campbell made a questionable decision at the end of the half to not try to push for points, which ultimately allowed Wisconsin to win the middle eight of the game.

On offense, there were multiple third-and-longs where Taylor Mouser decided to run the ball, which led to punts. However, the defense was the standout unit of the game, with D’Anton Lynn’s unit shutting down Wisconsin for the most part until the final two drives.

Offense: D

The offense could barely do anything during the game, combining for 233 total yards. Neither the pass game nor run game found any rhythm throughout the game, leading to only six points scored from drives the offense had to put together.

Passing game: F

Rocco Becht was out of rhythm the entire game, connecting on 41% of his passes. He only completed passes to three different players, tight end Benjamin Brahmer, running back Quinton Martin Jr. and wide receiver Chase Sowell.

With the absence of Koby Howard, Becht couldn’t find other weapons to make up for it, and the passing game wasn’t able to get anything going during the game.

Run game: D+

While the run game also wasn’t great, it was better than the pass game. Running back James Peoples emerged as the top running back in Week 4, with 14 carries for 67 yards.

As a whole, the run game totaled 3.3 yards per carry, which was significantly down from a week ago, mainly due to the lack of explosive runs.

Offensive line: C+

The protection for Becht held up pretty well throughout the game no matter the looks Wisconsin’s defense gave. Becht was sacked twice during the game, but other than that, the line gave the quarterback time to throw the ball.

In the run game it was a little different, as the holes on some occasions weren’t there. Down inside the 5-yard line, Martin was stuffed without anywhere to run in an opportunity for the line to force its will against Wisconsin’s defense.

Defense: C

Until the fourth quarter, the defense was the reason Penn State had a lead. When it started to fall apart is when Wisconsin pounced and took the lead late in the game. With the mix of the first three quarters and the final one, an even C grade seems logical given the circumstances.

Pass rush: F

The pass rush was borderline nonexistent. Wisconsin’s offensive line isn’t anything great, but the pressure on quarterback Colton Joseph only showed up when the Nittany Lions sent extra rushers.

Joseph was sacked once by linebacker Tony Rojas, who doesn’t rush the passer on every play, and that sack didn’t even occur in the backfield. The lack of pressure it caused on the pass game from the likes of Yvan Kemajou and Ike Ezeogu is worrisome as the season goes along.

Secondary: B-

The secondary was the standout unit of the team throughout the first three quarters. Cornerback Josiah Zayas had a pick six in the second quarter and cornerback Daryus Dixson picked off Joseph on the following drive.

Audavion Collins led the way with three passes broken up as he shut down any receiver he was covering. However, the secondary was part of the gashing Wisconsin did at the end of the game, dropping the grade from what would’ve likely been an A.

Linebackers: B+

The linebackers had the best all around game. Between Rojas, Kooper Ebel and Alex Tatsch — who were the main three linebackers to play — they flew around the field.

Ebel was tied for the lead in tackles with eight, while Rojas was just behind him with six, including a sack and an interception. There wasn’t much more the linebacker core could’ve done to try to will Penn State to a win.

Special teams: A-

The special teams unit was consistent throughout the game. Ryan Barker went a perfect 2-for-2 on field goals.

The kickoff specialists have been dominant in their category all season. Between Cristiano Rosa and Lucas Tenbrock, they combined for four touchbacks and allowed one return that went for 20 yards.

Wide receiver Zay Robinson had a lighter return game, but he gave Penn State good field position after the defense pinned Wisconsin deep.

Punter Nathan Tiyce got his most work of the season, punting seven times for an average of 42.7 yards. This included two punts inside the 20-yard line.

title: No. 14 Penn State women's volleyball upset by Michigan State in 4 sets
author: Ashley Felsberg I The Daily Collegian
description:
After a 3-1 win against Michigan on Friday, Penn State continued its action Sunday against Michigan State.

The Nittany Lions couldn’t continue their winning ways, falling 3-1.

Kennedy Martin opened up the match with a kill from the right side, giving Penn State the early lead. Michigan State’s Hayley Ogden quickly answered back to even out the playing field. After a quick couple of back-and-forths, the Spartans broke through for a five-point run, taking an 11-6 lead.

The Spartans continued to go on multiple three-point runs to keep the point gap to at least five. When the score reached 19-10, Michigan State had totaled 13 kills and not a single error.

Martin gave the Nittany Lions their 13th point after a central kill. Her momentum continued after another kill. Martin and Ryla Jones combined for a right-side block, bringing the blue and white within five and forcing Michigan State into a timeout.

Following the timeout, the Nittany Lions scored five straight points. A serving error from Ava Falduto returned offensive control to Michigan State; however, Martin quickly reversed it with a solo block.

Back-and-forth play continued until Alanna Bankston earned the Spartans their 23rd point following a powerful kill for her fifth of the set. While it seemed Penn State had a promising comeback, Michigan State continued with back-to-back aces to take set one.

Gabrielle Nichols’ block gave Penn State the first point of set two. Jones contributed three kills of her own, her third giving Penn State its ninth point, while also forcing Michigan State to take its second timeout.

As Michigan State slowly started to creep back in, Penn State was able to extend its lead. Alexis Stucky assisted Martin in a cross-court swing for the blue and white’s 13th point, but a Stucky attack error kept Michigan State within one.

The Spartans took the lead on back-to-back kills from Carmen Waye. After a service error, two attack errors for Penn State and a Michigan State ace, the Spartans extended their lead to four.

After Bankston and Waye contributed a paired block and Malayah Long added an ace of her own, the Spartans lead extended to six points. Waye followed up with a kill, extending the unanswered run to seven.

Whitney Launstein attempted to give Penn State a final push of momentum, contributing two kills to bring the blue and white within five. This aided a spark as a Nichols block, and a Waye attack error added two more points.

Jones committed a service error, putting Michigan State within two of set point. Madi Andrews added a kill for Michigan State, but it was called a lift. Andrews then followed up with another kill, as did Zora Hardison.

The Nittany Lions stayed alive after Launstein answered back with a central kill, however Hardison responded, and Michigan State took set two.

The Spartans opened up set three with a five point run, as Penn State struggled with the serve receive. Coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley called a timeout, yet Michigan State earned the first two points following the stoppage.

Penn State earned its first point after an attack error by Andrews. Martin followed with a kill of her own, yet Ogden responded to halt the momentum. The Spartans lead was halved after a successful Martin attack and an error by Michigan State.

The Nittany Lions closed the gap to three after a block from freshman, Daniella Whitemire. Sellman’s one time swing aided Penn State’s four point run, however a kill by Hardison halted this comeback. Bankston then brought Michigan State to double digits, with a same-side kill.

The Spartans lead was pulled back to three after Martin contributed a kill to the back side of the court. Each time Penn State crawled within the three-point range, the Spartans answered back, this time with an Andrews kill.

When the score reached 14-11, Jones went down, after colliding with teammate Falduto. She headed out for the remainder of the match, and the officials called for a point-redo. Penn State fought for the point, after an attack error from Waye.

Michigan State earned the 15th point through a left-side hit from Andrews, as the game headed into a media timeout.

Penn State evened the score at 16-16 after a Martin kill. The Nittany Lions battled head to head for the next two points, taking the lead on an Andrews attack error.

Penn State briefly kept its lead, as a Martin attack error balanced out the score. The two teams traded one point leads until Penn State earned a two point upper-hand with a Martin kill and Bankston attack error.

The score flipped in favor of the Spartans after they went on a three-point run, forcing Schumacher-Cawley to use another timeout. The Nittany Lions took the lead with attacks from Nichols and Martin.

An attack error from the Spartans brought the blue and white to set point, yet coach Kristen Kelsay burned her last challenge, looking for an illegal attack fault. The challenge was unsuccessful and the call stood, keeping the score at 24-22.

Martin put up her 14th kill of the day to aid the first set win for the blue and white.

The fourth set started differently, as the Spartans didn’t build a big lead early and the teams traded one- and two-point leads.

After the third point for Michigan State, the Spartans continued the lead for the remainder of the set.

Michigan State called a late set timeout after Penn State went on a three-point run, bringing the blue and white within three points of a completed comeback. Following the timeout, Ava Jurevicius contributed an ace.

Back-to-back errors from the Nittany Lions put the Spartans one away from match point. Penn State used a timeout for one last chance of a regrouping to aid an offensive spark.

Ogden extended the set with a kill following the timeout, bringing the blue and white to within six points. Long added another Spartan attack error to close the gap to five; however, Martin's attack error clinched the match for Michigan State.

Injury Report

Jones left the game in set three with a lower-body injury and didn’t return.

Up Next

Penn State returns home on Thursday at 7 p.m. for its match against No. 1 Nebraska.

title: Penn State drops out of AP Top 25
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian

Penn State has been kicked out of the AP Poll after a climatic upset in the Big Ten opener.

The Nittany Lions are now unranked in the wake of their 24-20 loss to Wisconsin on Saturday, the program’s first defeat at the hands of the Badgers since 2011. It was also Wisconsin’s first win at Beaver Stadium since 2003.

Across the Big Ten, Ohio State moved up to No. 5, Iowa rose to No. 14 and Michigan fell out of the top 25 after the Hawkeyes beat the Wolverines 20-19, Oregon advanced to No. 15 and USC dropped to No. 18 after the Ducks won 41-27. Indiana fell to No. 6 after a close win over Northwestern.

title: How improbable was Penn State’s loss to Wisconsin?
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State held leads of 17-0 and 20-10 during the game and seemingly had the game in control.

Despite that, Wisconsin marched down the field on big-play bursts to mount the comeback and defeat Penn State, against all odds.

How improbable was this loss?

In-game probability

On Wisconsin quarterback Colton Joseph’s third interception, Penn State’s chances to win peaked on ESPN’s win probability metric. The Nittany Lions had a 98.5% win probability with eight minutes left.

After Joseph’s touchdown pass to wide receiver Eugene Hilton Jr., Penn State still had a win probability of 89.1%, as it just needed about two first downs to put the game away.

The Nittany Lions went three-and-out, but the Badgers weren’t doing everything to take the game that Penn State was essentially handing them. A false start on tight end Jacob Harris put the Nittany Lions’ win probability up to 89.4%.

Harris would ultimately catch a pass and go the distance that flipped the probability in Wisconsin’s favor.

Breaking tradition

The loss was even more improbable than just the ESPN metric. Since 2002, Penn State had held a 17-point lead 101 times in Beaver Stadium. In those games, the Nittany Lions were 101-0 until Saturday night.

Even with all of that against it, the Nittany Lions have also had Wisconsin’s number in the last 15 years. Saturday was the first time the Badgers have defeated Penn State since 2011, when a Russell Wilson-led Wisconsin team won against Penn State, 45-7.

Wilson wasn’t the quarterback out on the field on Saturday. Prior to the final two drives, Joseph was a measly 10-of-22 with a 45% completion percentage, and his numbers didn’t even take much of a jump as the Badgers came back to win.

In addition to Joseph’s lackluster numbers, the Badgers were without their leading rusher, Abu Sama III. He went down with an injury in the second quarter, but backup running back Darrion Dupree was key in the comeback.

History for Wisconsin

Joseph and Dupree led Wisconsin to its largest comeback since 2006 and snapped a 64-game winning streak for the Nittany Lions in games it led by 10 or more points entering the fourth quarter. It was also Wisconsin’s first road win since 2024.

The 17-point lead is tied for the largest blown lead Matt Campbell has had during his head coaching career. It’s also the largest blown lead by a Penn State team since 2017, when it led Ohio State 21-3 in the second quarter.

Campbell said Penn State “left it to chance,” and against all odds, chance came out in Wisconsin’s favor.
