title: Column | Penn State’s TEs are supposedly the ‘heartbeat’ of the offense. So, where are they?
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
Benjamin Brahmer has said multiple times Taylor Mouser believes the tight end room is the “heartbeat” of Penn State’s offense.

So, where were they Saturday?

Brahmer caught three passes for 33 yards across the Nittany Lions’ first two drives. He moved the chains twice. It looked like in Koby Howard’s absence, Mouser was turning to his 6-foot-7 tight end that was a John Mackey Award finalist last season.

Brahmer didn’t catch another pass until the fourth quarter.

In the time between his third catch and his fourth, Penn State had turned 17-0 and 20-10 leads into a three-point game. It couldn’t get anything going on offense, and wide receiver Chase Sowell was the only other pass-catcher with a reception.

“I think there was just a weird flow to the game, especially in the first half of the football game, where you're in more situational football,” Matt Campbell said postgame. “I think some of it will be really interesting to see what happened in the second half. We're going to have to have more production from the receiving room and from the other players on the opposite side of the ball.”

Mouser has also talked at length about how much he loves Gabe Burkle and was frustrated with him being limited against Temple. Burkle only has one catch this year.

And then there’s Andrew Rappleyea, who had one target against Wisconsin on the second-to-last play of the game. He had a chance to bring it in for the game-winning score, but he jumped slightly too soon and it fell incomplete.

As a whole, the tight end room has 215 yards this season, good for about 54 yards a game. In theory, that’s not bad. But with the talent at Mouser’s disposal there, it’s not where it should be.

It’s understandable for the tight ends to not see as many targets with Howard in the lineup, as he’s far and away the best playmaker Penn State has on offense.

But Howard wasn’t available against Wisconsin, and he seemingly won’t be suiting up for at least the next two games based on the Instagram story he posted earlier in the week. So the Nittany Lions need to get production in the passing game from someone else.

“I'd be a fool to sit up here and say we didn't miss Koby,” Campbell said. “I would also say I have great belief in the rest of our guys, and the rest of our guys had some opportunities, and they got to keep pounding away at it.”

That someone else should be Brahmer. He can tower over opposing defenses and is good at finding space and hauling in contested catches, even if Howard is still better at that specifically.

Brahmer is supposed to be one of the best tight ends in the country this season, and he should be treated by his offensive coordinator as such. Yes, tight ends are important for blocking purposes, even more so when the run game is struggling like it is now, but Brahmer is too good of a pass-catcher to not be utilized.

So moving forward, Mouser has to get the ball to the so-called “heartbeat” of his offense. Especially with Howard out. And especially after Saturday’s offensive performance.

“I think it's on me to spread the ball out,” Rocco Becht said. “We just got to be better on all of our parts. To go out there and make plays when they're there to be made. So again, I put that on me. I got to be able to spread the ball around and be able to make the defense guess.”

title: Penn State’s 4th quarter defensive collapse against Wisconsin was ‘self-inflicted’
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Down 20-17, Wisconsin quarterback Colton Joseph found Jacob Harris deep up the middle with 1:13 remaining in the game. Harris had only cornerback Audavion Collins to beat and shed the tackle en route to a game-winning 72-yard touchdown.

The Homecoming game crowd at Beaver Stadium on Saturday night was speechless. Not only did Penn State lose its Big Ten opener, but it did so with a shocking defensive collapse in the fourth quarter.

“Defensively, I thought we played a tremendous football game,” Matt Campbell said postgame. “We gave ourselves every opportunity to win, and we didn’t take advantage.”

The Nittany Lions led 17-0 with under two minutes remaining in the first half, and that goose egg on the scoreboard wasn’t without good reason. Cornerbacks Josiah Zayas and Daryus Dixson had back-to-back interceptions in the second quarter, key to the convincing lead.

Zayas first jumped a pass along the flat and ran 51 yards into the end zone for a pick six, the first touchdown of the game before Dixson capitalized on an overthrown pass.

“It's nothing new,” linebacker Kooper Ebel said. “We see that every week, every day at practice. It's a tribute to how they show up and work every day.”

However, momentum flipped when Joseph scored a 7-yard rushing touchdown going into halftime. Penn State wasn’t immortal any longer.

“Obviously we wouldn't have liked to let that up,” linebacker Kooper Ebel said. “We talk about momentum all the time, we talk about winning the middle eight. They did a great job of executing there at the end of the half.”

Cracks had begun to show throughout the second half as Joseph found strings of success but couldn’t finish the job. There were pockets of big gains that proved Wisconsin could take advantage of opportunities, and when Penn State started to make mistakes, the Badgers did just that.

“It was self-inflicted,” safety Jeremiah Cooper said. “We just got to get better at everything we messed up on.”

Ebel echoed that sentiment. He said there were issues with finishing plays because of “pre-snap alignment,” and said the noise volume inside Beaver Stadium was a factor in limiting communication between the defenders.

Wisconsin got the job done late in the fourth quarter after relentlessly pushing forward despite facing immense adversity. Cooper said postgame the main issue was with “fundamental techniques.”

Although Tony Rojas’ fourth-quarter interception made it seem like Penn State had everything under control, D’Anton Lynn’s defense completely unraveled in the Badgers’ final two drives of the game.

It began with an 11-yard touchdown pass to Eugene Hilton Jr., that was by no means an easy grab. Hilton had to toe-tap the side of the end zone and hold on to a ball thrown over his shoulder after blazing by Marcus Neal Jr.

“I know it was on Marcus,” Cooper said. “But I know Marcus is a much better player than that. I know he's gonna fix that, so I have full confidence that he's gonna bounce back from that.”

The next drive was when Harris went the distance to win the game.

Despite the offense’s apparent struggles to capitalize on the chances the defense generated, Cooper made sure to take accountability for the loss, citing that “it’s team football at the end of the day.”

“We still let them score,” Cooper said. “So it's not on them. It's on us.”

title: ‘I’ve got to be better’ | Penn State’s offense struggles amidst season-lows from Rocco Becht, WRs
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
With five seconds left on the clock, Rocco Becht launched the ball to the end zone, needing a touchdown while trailing 24-20.

But similar to his performance through the previous 59 minutes, the deep ball wasn’t there, as it sailed out of the end zone to clinch Penn State’s first loss of the season against Wisconsin.

“I got to be better for this team,” Becht said. “I can’t put us in scenarios where our backs are backed up and we got to have a big play. I didn’t do my part today, so I got to do better.”

It was a season-low performance for the winningest active quarterback in college football. For the first time this season, he didn’t have a passing touchdown and threw his first interception of the year.

“It wasn't a ball that was a bad or poor decision,” Matt Campbell said postgame of Becht’s interception. “It was a tipped pass. I really thought Rocco played well. I thought it was a really good football game for the most part. I'll answer that better after I watch the tape.”

Becht finished just 12-for-29 for 114 yards in Penn State’s 233-yard offensive performance. The Nittany Lions’ offense only found the end zone once, as Becht recorded his first rushing touchdown of the season.

But Penn State’s quarterback was missing his top target, as Koby Howard is currently sidelined for an “extended period of time.” It was clear throughout the game that Becht and the offense missed Howard out there.

“I'd be a fool to sit up here and say, man, we didn't miss Koby,” Matt Campbell said postgame. “Koby's a guy that we all have great faith in.”

Throughout the week, there was a lot of talk of the other wide receivers stepping up. Chase Sowell, Brett Eskildsen and Zay Robinson were all names that were expected to see more targets, while freshman wide receiver Amarion Jackson was also discussed as a potential contributor.

Instead, Sowell was the only wide receiver who recorded a reception against Wisconsin. The former Iowa State receiver had six catches for 70 yards, including a handful of plays in big moments for the Nittany Lions.

“I would say I'm a little bit surprised that that is the statistic in the game,” Campbell said. “We're going to have to have more production from the receiver room, from the other players on the offensive side of the football.”

Eskildsen was back at full strength after being banged up over the past two weeks, but didn’t record a catch. He was almost involved in the passing game many times, as Becht targeted him on several deep balls.

However, Eskildsen wasn’t able to haul any of them in, albeit some were underthrown, including what could’ve been a touchdown late in the game.

“I saw the defense, the corner, kind of stutter his feet, and Brett got behind him. I got to put a better ball out there,” Becht said. “I got to make it easier on these receivers to go out there and make plays.”

While Becht had those struggles in the passing game, Campbell said “some of our issues were probably more so with some protection things.”

Becht faced immense pressure from Wisconsin’s pass rush, which recorded two sacks and two quarterback hits.

At one point, right tackle and captain Anthony Donkoh was subject to a spin move from a Wisconsin defender, who ran unguarded at Becht. There were numerous times he had to scramble out of the pocket and throw the ball away.

“I feel like this game, we have a lot of responsibility,” left guard Trevor Buhr said. “I really just feel like in all those moments and everything, we got to do everything we can to help all those other guys and try to have those guys be able to lean on us. We just gotta get better.”

After scoring just one offensive touchdown and three second-half points against Wisconsin, Campbell stressed the significance of coming back and going head first into next week’s game against Northwestern.

“The reality of it is, these are all correctable things if we’re willing and humble enough to be able to make the corrections,” Campbell said. “It’ll be a great challenge for us. Not going to be easy, but we look forward to the challenge.”

title: Penn State players see growth opportunity following loss to Wisconsin
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State suffered its first loss of the season, and first under Matt Campbell, in dramatic fashion after giving up two touchdowns in the fourth quarter.

Despite the loss, the team felt it was an opportunity to grow and rally together to push forward, especially given the Nittany Lions have a short week with a road matchup against Northwestern on Friday.

“We just got to learn from this, and we got a great opportunity to bounce back next week with this quick week, and we just got to take everything that we learned from this game,” offensive lineman Trevor Buhr said. “It's pretty good we got some adversity at this point, so just taking everything we can learn from this and then applying it forward.”

The players and coaching staff made sure to keep each other’s heads up following the loss to avoid dwelling on what happened on the field.

Running back James Peoples recognized that “moment to grow” during his conversation with running back coach Savon Huggins postgame as they walked off the field.

That mentality was heard throughout the locker room, as Campbell’s message to the team more so focused on keeping spirits high than the collapse to end the game.

“Win or loss, we're going to come in tomorrow and continue to work, and I think that's just the attitude and the message that he gives us is to continue to just push forward and be ourselves and go out there and compete,” Rocco Becht said.

Buhr noticed the same thing when offensive line coach Ryan Clanton addressed his players after the game. Buhr said Clanton told the offensive line that there’s still “a lot of football left” and to plan to “bounce back tomorrow and just get ready and keep moving forward.”

What stood out the most to the players was Becht’s message to the team in the locker room despite his performance. Becht had an underwhelming day with 129 passing yards and a 41% completion percentage, but he still spoke to the team and kept the spirits high.

“He was very motivated because I think he feels like all the pressure is on him and all the blows on him,” defensive tackle Armstrong Nnodim said. “Just for him to come to the team and just speak highly of everything, it shows his character and through adversity, he can still remain positive.”

Kicker Ryan Barker said the team has already begun focusing on Northwestern and “kind of flushed it, and that's what we have to do when we face adversity.”

The team will still look at the film on Sunday and address what went well and went wrong throughout the game to help it continue forward. Buhr is “really not concerned about (the loss) at all,” knowing there’s still eight games left in the season.

“You gotta keep your head up,” safety Jeremiah Cooper said. “It's literally the first conference game, and we got a whole season to play. So it's keeping our head up.”

title: 3 takeaways from Penn State's shocking loss to Wisconsin
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State kicked off the first Big Ten slate under Matt Campbell with a home game against Wisconsin in front of a Helmet Stripe crowd.

The Nittany Lions lost their first game of the season to Wisconsin despite three interceptions from the defense throughout the game.

Here’s three takeaways from Penn State’s loss.

Defense collapses late

Penn State’s defense limited Wisconsin to 124 total yards in the first half and forced two turnovers that led to two touchdowns.

In the fourth quarter, the defense collapsed, allowing Wisconsin to make a comeback after being down by 10.

Wisconsin began its first touchdown drive of the quarter with 7:02 left in the game. Running back Darrion Dupree gashed Penn State’s defense, with gains of 17, 13 and 10 yards to get the Badgers into the Nittany Lions’ territory.

After allowing a 13-yard touchdown pass, the defense was tasked with making one final stop with 2:28 left on the clock, and it was gashed once again.

A 72-yard touchdown to tight end Jacob Harris gave Wisconsin the lead with over a minute left. The total collapse of the defense after previously shutting down the Badgers’ offense could’ve come from the lack of time it had off the field.

“I think we had a guy slip on the broken play, and one slip, and that play, that situation, it's kind of like the narrative of the second half, right?” Campbell said. “We left it to chance, and we had so many opportunities to put the game away.”

Penn State’s offense had three straight three-and-outs, giving the defense very little time to rest. The defensive collapse led to Wisconsin’s upset victory over the Nittany Lions in comeback fashion.

Pass rush can’t get success

The pass rush gave Joseph plenty of time to throw the ball. It was a concern entering the game, and it remains a concern after recording just one sack.

Additionally, that sack came from linebacker Tony Rojas, who had to run across the field to get to Joseph.

With that much time in the pocket, Joseph was able to sit and find receivers who got themselves open. When D’Anton Lynn dialed up a blitz, it was able to bring pressure on Joseph and force him to make an errant throw.

Despite the struggles Joseph showed when pressure was in his face, the pass rush didn’t get to him very often. Joseph wasn’t able to beat Penn State through the air much, though, thanks to the secondary shutting down Wisconsin’s receivers.

Penn State’s edge rushers are going to have to find success more often as the season continues, as the level of offenses is only going to get better.

Penn State’s offense struggles without Koby Howard

Penn State seemingly had plenty of weapons to rely on with the absence of Koby Howard.

However, those weapons weren’t showcased in the loss over Wisconsin, as the offense scored just 13 points, with 10 of them from the defense giving it good field position.

“We really struggled to find the rhythm and I think in the first half, we were either backup or on the goal line and we never got into the flow of the game, and I feel like it kind of led into the second half of the football game and kind of being in the same spot because we struggled,” Campbell said.

Tight end Benjamin Brahmer was utilized early, catching three passes when the offense was moving the ball in the first quarter, but he wasn’t targeted after that despite being Rocco Becht’s largest target.

After 304 rushing yards in Week 3 against Buffalo, the run game didn’t show much, running for an average of 3.4 yards per carry. James Peoples led the way with 67 yards on the ground.

In the air, Becht connected with just three receivers, with the missing big-play ability from Howard giving the rest of the weapons less favorable opportunities in the pass game.

The offense was stagnant throughout the game and kept Wisconsin in the game, allowing it to mount the comeback and defeat the Nittany Lions.

title: TE Andrew Rappleyea, C Brock Riker game-time decisions in Penn State's game availability report
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State has released its final availability report of the week.

Ahead of the 5 p.m. start, center Brock Riker and tight end Andrew Rappleyea are both game-time decisions.

Safety Omarion Davis, wide receiver Ethan Black and offensive lineman Dom Rulli are also listed as game-time decisions ahead of the Nittany Lions' first Big Ten game.

No additional players have been ruled out, with wide receiver Koby Howard and linebacker Cam Smith headlining the players who'll miss Saturday's game.

Defensive ends Lavar Arrington II, Mason Robinson, Dayshaun Burnett and Max Granville will also be out. Cornerbacks Joshua Johnson, Christian Askew and Tyler Armstead have also been ruled out, with offensive lineman Will Tompkins and tight end Cooper Alexander rounding out the group who'll miss the Big Ten opener against Wisconsin.

Tompkins and Granville are confirmed to have season-ending injuries.

author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
The start of Big Ten play features a new captain for Penn State.

Audavion Collins is the newest captain for the Nittany Lions, joining Rocco Becht, Anthony Donkoh and Kooper Ebel.
